claims.claim: Guinness World Records officially named the honey badger the world's most fearless animal
claims.sourceCitation: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI), Animal of the Week: Honey Badger (Mellivora capensis)
claims.note: SANBI attributes the title to the 2002 edition of the Guinness Book of World Records. It is a retired print-edition accolade, not a currently listed Guinness record - I searched guinnessworldrecords.com and found no active entry. The article's present tense ('officially named it') implies a live record; 'was named in the 2002 Guinness Book of World Records' would be accurate.

claims.claim: Honey badgers (Mellivora capensis) are members of the weasel family, native to Africa, the Middle East, and parts of South Asia
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: IUCN lists family Mustelidae, subfamily Mellivorinae. Range extends through sub-Saharan Africa, Arabia, Iran, western Asia to Turkmenistan/Uzbekistan, the Indian peninsula and Nepal.

claims.claim: They weigh somewhere between 9 and 35 pounds
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: Mammalian Species gives African males mean 9.2 kg (range 7.7-10.5) and females mean 8.9 kg (range 6.2-13.6); Asian animals are smaller. Documented span is roughly 13-30 lb, with field-guide maxima to 16 kg (35 lb) for large males. The 9 lb low end is a little below any measured adult, but the range is broadly defensible.

claims.claim: They stand about a foot tall
claims.sourceCitation: South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI), Animal of the Week: Honey Badger (Mellivora capensis)
claims.note: SANBI gives shoulder height of approximately 25-30 cm, which is 10-12 inches.

claims.claim: The hide of a honey badger is extraordinarily thick (up to 6mm in some places), rubbery, and remarkably loose on the body
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: 'Near the throat, skin is 6 mm thick (Kingdon 1977).' The 6 mm figure is specific to the neck/throat region, so 'in some places' is the correct framing.

claims.claim: When a predator grabs a honey badger by the scruff, the animal can twist around inside its own skin and bite its attacker
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: Skin is 'tough, thick, and loose, preventing a predator from firmly grasping it and allowing honey badgers to turn in their skin and bite the attacker.'

claims.claim: Lions, leopards, and hyenas have all learned the hard way that getting a grip on a honey badger does not mean you have won the fight
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: IUCN states the reverse: 'Large carnivores such as Lion (Panthera leo) and Leopard (Panthera pardus) prey on Honey Badger adults and cubs, while cubs are also killed by Black-backed Jackals.' Begg et al. 2005 recorded two cases where a mother and cub were killed together by large predators, and the remains of a young male in a hyaena den. Adult annual mortality was 34%.

claims.claim: The skin is tough enough to resist bee stings, porcupine quills, and even machete blows in some documented cases
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: The species account says skin is 'impervious to stings of bees, fangs of snakes, and teeth of dogs,' but sources it to Blumenbach 1825 and Stevenson-Hamilton 1947 - century-old anecdote, not measurement. Porcupine quills are claimed in secondary literature citing Rosevear 1974. I found no source at all for machete blows; that appears to be internet folklore.

claims.claim: They regularly hunt and eat venomous snakes, including cobras and puff adders
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2003. Sexual and seasonal variation in the diet and foraging behaviour of a sexually dimorphic carnivore, the honey badger (Mellivora capensis). Journal of Zoology 260:301-316
claims.note: Over 3,324 observed food items, puff adder (Bitis arietans) contributed 12.5% and Cape cobra (Naja nivea) 10.5% of biomass; mole snake 21.4%. 'All small mammals, small reptiles and large reptiles were eaten entirely, including the heads of poisonous snakes.'

claims.claim: Their diet includes mambas
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2003. Journal of Zoology 260:301-316
claims.note: The only detailed prey list in the literature (59 species, southern Kalahari) records mole snake, Cape cobra, puff adder, horned adder, sand snakes, quill-snouted snake and juvenile African rock python, but no mamba. Mambas are outside the Kalahari study area so this is plausible but undocumented.

claims.claim: After being bitten, a honey badger might collapse, go limp, and appear dead for a short time. Then it wakes up, shakes it off, and goes right back to eating the snake
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C. & Begg, K., The Honey Badger Research Project (Mellivora capensis)
claims.note: The Beggs' own field record is that a honey badger bitten on the face by a puff adder 'showed signs of severe pain but recovered fully within five hours.' That is hours of serious envenomation, not a brief nap. The site also hedges the biology: honey badgers 'do appear to have some immunity to snake venoms.'

claims.claim: Researchers believe this resistance comes from genetic mutations in the honey badger's nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, the same type of adaptation seen in other venom-resistant animals like mongooses
claims.sourceCitation: Drabeck, D.H., Dean, A.M. & Jansa, S.A. 2015. Why the honey badger don't care: Convergent evolution of venom-targeted nicotinic acetylcholine receptors in mammals that survive venomous snake bites. Toxicon 99:68-72
claims.note: Three problems. (1) The paper identifies hedgehogs and pigs as sharing the honey badger's specific amino-acid replacement; mongooses modify the same receptor by a different route (glycosylation). (2) The receptor targeted is the binding site for elapid alpha-neurotoxins - cobras and mambas. It does not explain surviving puff adder bites, since puff adders are vipers with cytotoxic venom acting by a completely different mechanism. The article presents one mechanism as covering both. (3) The resistance was inferred from phylogenetic sequence analysis, not functionally tested.

claims.claim: Honey badgers will tear into active beehives with zero hesitation, enduring thousands of stings to get to the larvae and honey inside. The bees sting. The honey badger does not care
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2003. Journal of Zoology 260:301-316
claims.note: The only quantified field observation says the opposite. Two honey badgers were watched breaking into 13 bee hives over 37 visits, and 'On 61% of the visits the swarm's defence was sufficient to chase off the honey badgers.' Separately, study animals were 'twice observed to unsuccessfully attempt to break into bee hives.' The bees win the majority of encounters.

claims.claim: They are opportunistic and relentless foragers, covering up to 25 miles a day in search of food
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: The highest figure in the literature is ca. 27 km/day (about 17 miles) for males and ca. 10 km/day for females (Kruuk & Mills 1983). 25 miles is 40 km, which no source supports. Begg et al. 2003 further dispute the framing, finding both sexes are short-distance foragers when actually hunting, and that long-distance walking by males is mostly social (latrine checking, searching for females), yielding under 10% of intake.

claims.claim: Their powerful claws can be over an inch long
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: Forefoot nails average ca. 32 mm, the middle claw ca. 38 mm, the smallest outer one 25 mm. One inch is 25.4 mm, so 'over an inch' is correct.

claims.claim: Their jaws are strong enough to crush bone and even turtle shells
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: No published bite-force measurement for Mellivora capensis exists that I could locate; the figures circulating online (216.9 N / 160 psi) trace only to content-farm aggregators. The species account also describes a different mechanism for shells: 'carapaces of turtles... are peeled away to expose the softer inner parts,' i.e. worked open with claws rather than crushed in the jaws.

claims.claim: The greater honeyguide actively seeks out a honey badger, calls to get its attention, and leads it to a beehive; a genuine mutualistic relationship, one of the few well-documented examples of interspecies cooperation involving a wild bird and a wild mammal, observed and documented for centuries
claims.sourceCitation: van der Wal, J.E.M. et al. 2023. Do honey badgers and greater honeyguide birds cooperate to access bees' nests? Ecological evidence and honey-hunter accounts. Journal of Zoology 321:22-32
claims.note: This is the article's biggest error. The definitive review, by 25 authors including the Beggs and Spottiswoode, drawing on the published literature, the authors' own fieldwork on both species, and 394 honey-hunter interviews across nine African countries, concludes: 'We find that the scientific evidence relies on incomplete and second-hand accounts and does not convincingly indicate that the two species cooperate.' The famous footage everyone has seen, from the 1974 film 'Animals Are Beautiful People,' 'was in fact entirely staged using a tame badger trained to follow a taxidermic model of a bird on a fishing line.' Lead author van der Wal: 'we've been guided to bees' nests by honeyguide birds thousands of times, but none of us have ever seen a bird and a badger interact.' The 2003 Mammalian Species account had already noted that a complete observation of the sequence 'does not exist.' The honest version is that the interaction may occur but is highly localized or extremely hard to observe, and remains unproven.

claims.claim: In some parts of Africa, people have learned to follow the honeyguide to find wild honey
claims.sourceCitation: Spottiswoode, C.N., Begg, K.S. & Begg, C.M. 2016. Reciprocal signaling in honeyguide-human mutualism. Science 353:387-389
claims.note: Well established and experimentally demonstrated. A specialized call by Mozambican honey-hunters raised the probability of being guided from about 33% to 66% and of finding a nest from 17% to 54%. Note the irony: the human-honeyguide partnership is real and rigorously proven, while the honey badger version is the unsupported one.

claims.claim: Honey badgers have well-developed anal scent glands and can evert the gland to release a powerful, suffocating odor
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: Two anal glands, each ca. 30 by 20 mm; secretion is yellow, resembles liquid mustard, and its smell is perceptible at 45 m. 'Anal pouch is everted whenever honey badgers become excited (Kingdon 1977); fluid is dribbled, not squirted (Estes 1991).' The dribbling detail undercuts the article's 'deploy a stink bomb on demand' framing slightly.

claims.claim: The scent glands may have some effect on calming bees during hive raids
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: 'Anal secretions may be used to fumigate insects when robbing nests of bees.' This is a hypothesis attributed to Kingdon, not a demonstrated effect. The article's hedging ('may help,' 'thought to') is appropriate and should be kept.

claims.claim: Brian Jones, a wildlife rehabilitator in South Africa, kept a honey badger named Stoffel who used sticks and rocks as tools to escape enclosures
claims.sourceCitation: Earth Touch News Network, 'It's time to figure out just how smart honey badgers really are'
claims.note: The Stoffel account is real and filmed (BBC, 'Honey Badgers: Masters of Mayhem'), with Jones at the Moholoholo rehabilitation centre stating the behaviour was untrained. But it is a single captive animal documented on film, not a study.

claims.claim: This kind of flexible, innovative problem-solving is associated with high cognitive ability; in captivity they have been observed using tools, manipulating latches, and demonstrating creative intelligence
claims.sourceCitation: Earth Touch News Network, 'It's time to figure out just how smart honey badgers really are'
claims.note: 'There are simply no studies of honey badger cognition anywhere in the scientific literature,' and the reputation for intelligence 'is based solely on anecdote, not scientific study.' Cambridge primatologist William McGrew on the Stoffel footage: 'Either honey badgers have been under-estimated, or this is a one-off genius honey badger, or it is a hoax,' and recommended someone actually run problem-solving tasks. The article presents an untested reputation as established finding.

claims.claim: Honey badgers have relatively large brains for their body size
claims.sourceCitation: van der Wal, J.E.M. et al. 2023. Journal of Zoology 321:22-32
claims.note: 'Badgers have relatively large brains that may allow them to learn to exploit new food sources,' citing Benson-Amram et al. 2016 and Sheppey & Bernard 1984. Stated as background rather than as a new measurement, but it is a peer-reviewed statement.

claims.claim: They remember the locations of food sources and adapt their hunting strategies to different prey
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2003. Journal of Zoology 260:301-316
claims.note: One female developed an individual springhare-hunting technique (n=25) that her cub learned and used after independence; other habituated badgers ignored springhares entirely. Animals also revisited old solitary-bee-larvae sites in later years. The further claim of 'clear signs of planning and anticipation' is not supported by any study.

claims.claim: There are documented cases of honey badgers driving lions, leopards, and even small groups of wild dogs away from kills
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: IUCN supports the general behaviour - they 'may pirate food from other carnivores and will also scavenge from the kills of larger animals' - but names no species. I found no primary documentation of honey badgers displacing lions, leopards or wild dog packs specifically. The named list should be softened to the sourced generality.

claims.claim: They are remarkably fast and agile, able to climb trees and swim when needed
claims.sourceCitation: Vanderhaar, J.M. & Hwang, Y.T. 2003. Mellivora capensis. Mammalian Species 721:1-8
claims.note: Climbing and swimming are both supported ('Honey badgers are good swimmers and chase turtles underwater'; they ascend hollow trees and raid raptor nests). But speed is directly contradicted: 'Owing to the thickset form, stocky feet, and sharp and long foreclaws, honey badgers cannot run quickly. Their swinging trot or gallop is comparable with that of bears... a slow, rather bow-legged lumber, which they can maintain for hours.' They are enduring, not fast.

claims.claim: Females give birth to one or two cubs at a time
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2005. Life-history variables of an atypical mustelid, the honey badger Mellivora capensis. Journal of Zoology 265:17-22
claims.note: The species has 'the unusually small litter size of one cub.' Across 18 observed cases, only ever a single cub was seen with a female, and mothers were never observed moving more than one cub between dens. The paper explicitly rejects the older field-guide figures: it 'provides no evidence for the reported litter sizes of 1-4 cubs (mean = 2.5).' IUCN concurs: 'Small litter size (generally one cub).'

claims.claim: Cubs stay with their mothers for about a year and a half to two years
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2005. Journal of Zoology 265:17-22
claims.note: Independence occurs at 12-16 months (n=7, full range 12-22 months). Mean age at independence was 14.2 months for males and 14.6 months for females. 'A year and a half to two years' describes the top of the range as if it were typical.

claims.claim: Honey badgers are largely solitary animals, coming together mainly to mate, and den in burrows they dug themselves or took from another animal
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2005. Journal of Zoology 265:17-22
claims.note: 'The honey badger is a non-social species and only the mother rears the young'; adults did not cooperate in cub rearing, foraging or territory defence. The Mammalian Species account confirms they shelter in self-excavated dens or abandoned burrows of porcupines, yellow mongooses, aardvarks, bat-eared foxes, springhares and Cape foxes.

claims.claim: They are found from sub-Saharan Africa through the Arabian Peninsula and into India and Nepal, across forests, grasslands, deserts and mountains
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: India and Nepal both appear explicitly in the country-occurrence list. Habitat spans equatorial rainforest to Sahara/Namib desert margins, sea level to 2,600 m in the Moroccan High Atlas and 4,000 m in Ethiopia's Bale Mountains.

claims.claim: Honey badgers are primarily nocturnal where they face human pressure, but often active during the day in more remote areas
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: 'Honey Badgers are essentially nocturnal, but may be active during the day in areas where there is little human disturbance, and during seasons when day temperatures are cooler.' Accurate as written.

claims.claim: They are not currently considered endangered, though habitat loss and persecution by farmers pose localized threats
claims.sourceCitation: Do Linh San, E., Begg, C., Begg, K. & Abramov, A.V. 2016. Mellivora capensis. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2016: e.T41629A45210107
claims.note: Least Concern is correct, but the assessment records 'Current Population Trend: Decreasing' and warns that 'clearly identifiable threats are operating, and known to be resulting in localised declines.' It also notes 'evidence to suggest they have gone locally extinct in many areas through poisoning.' The dominant threat is direct persecution by beekeepers and small-livestock farmers using steel-jaw traps and poison, plus non-selective jackal and caracal control - not habitat loss, which the article lists first.

claims.claim: Their digging aerates soil and creates burrows that other animals use
claims.note: I found no study documenting honey badgers as ecosystem engineers or quantifying secondary use of their burrows. It is plausible by analogy with aardvarks and other diggers, but nothing in the primary literature supports it for this species. Either drop it or attribute it as a general property of burrowing carnivores.

claims.claim: Their predation on snakes keeps snake populations in check
claims.sourceCitation: Begg, C.M., Begg, K.S., Du Toit, J.T. & Mills, M.G.L. 2003. Journal of Zoology 260:301-316
claims.note: Snakes are confirmed as a major diet component by biomass, but no study has tested whether honey badger predation regulates snake population size. IUCN also notes honey badgers occur at low densities across most of their range (0.03 adults/km2 in the Kgalagadi), which makes strong top-down control unlikely. This is an inference, not a finding.

corrections.claim: The Honeyguide Bird: Nature's Odd Couple - the entire section asserting that the greater honeyguide leads honey badgers to hives, that this is 'a genuine mutualistic relationship, one of the few well-documented examples of interspecies cooperation involving a wild bird and a wild mammal,' and that it 'has been observed and documented by researchers and local communities for centuries.'
corrections.problem: This is the article's most serious error and it is backwards. The 2023 review in Journal of Zoology - 25 authors including the Beggs (who ran the only long-term honey badger field study) and Spottiswoode (who proved the human version) - drew on the published literature, their own fieldwork on both species, and 394 honey-hunter interviews in 11 communities across nine African countries, and concluded that 'the scientific evidence relies on incomplete and second-hand accounts and does not convincingly indicate that the two species cooperate.' 80% of communities surveyed had never seen it. The famous footage that fixed this story in popular culture, from the 1974 film 'Animals Are Beautiful People,' 'was in fact entirely staged using a tame badger trained to follow a taxidermic model of a bird on a fishing line,' confirmed by an original production staff member; that clip has since circulated online misrepresented as documentary footage. Even the 2003 Mammalian Species account noted a complete observation of the guiding sequence 'does not exist.' Meanwhile the article's throwaway final line - that people follow honeyguides to find honey - is the part that is actually rigorously established (Spottiswoode et al. 2016, Science).
corrections.suggestedFix: Rewrite the section around the real and more interesting story: the honeyguide-human partnership is genuine and experimentally proven, while the honeyguide-honey badger version is famous but unconfirmed. Something like: 'Here is one of the most repeated stories in nature writing, and one of the shakiest. The greater honeyguide (Indicator indicator) genuinely does lead people to beehives. That partnership is real, and researchers proved it experimentally in 2016: a specialized call used by Mozambican honey-hunters more than doubled the odds of being guided to a nest. The bird gets the wax and larvae, the people get the honey. The version you have probably heard, though, has the bird leading a honey badger. That one has never been confirmed. In 2023 a team of 25 researchers, including the biologists who ran the only long-term honey badger field study, reviewed the evidence and interviewed 394 honey-hunters across nine African countries. Their verdict: the scientific evidence rests on incomplete, second-hand accounts and does not convincingly show the two species cooperate. The lead author put it plainly, saying they have been guided to nests by honeyguides thousands of times and not one of them has ever seen a bird and a badger interact. And the famous film clip everyone shares? It came from a 1974 comic nature film and was entirely staged, using a tame honey badger trained to follow a stuffed bird dangled on a fishing line. Honey-hunters in a few Tanzanian communities, notably the Hadzabe, do report seeing it, so the interaction may well happen somewhere. It is just that after two centuries of stories, nobody has documented it.'

corrections.claim: Honey badgers will tear into active beehives with zero hesitation, enduring thousands of stings to get to the larvae and honey inside. The bees sting. The honey badger does not care.
corrections.problem: The only quantified field observation says the opposite. Begg et al. (2003) report two habituated study animals breaking into 13 bee hives over 37 visits, and 'On 61% of the visits the swarm's defence was sufficient to chase off the honey badgers.' The same study notes its animals were 'twice observed to unsuccessfully attempt to break into bee hives.' Bees repel honey badgers most of the time.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with something like: 'Honey badgers do raid active hives, and their thick hide takes a lot of the sting out of it. But the swagger is overstated. When researchers watched two badgers work 13 hives over 37 visits, the bees drove them off on 61% of attempts. They are persistent rather than invulnerable, and a well-defended colony usually wins.'

corrections.claim: Females give birth to one or two cubs at a time... Cubs stay with their mothers for about a year and a half to two years.
corrections.problem: Litter size is one cub, not one or two. Begg et al. (2005) describe 'the unusually small litter size of one cub'; across 18 observed cases only a single cub was ever seen, and the paper explicitly rejects the older field-guide figure of 1-4 cubs (mean 2.5). IUCN concurs: 'generally one cub.' Independence is 12-16 months (mean 14.2 months for males, 14.6 for females), not 18-24.
corrections.suggestedFix: 'Females give birth to a single cub, which is remarkably small for a mustelid and one reason honey badgers live at such low densities. Cubs are born in a burrow the mother dug herself, or borrowed from an aardvark, porcupine or fox, and stay with her for roughly 12 to 16 months, learning to dig, climb and hunt before striking out alone.'

corrections.claim: They are opportunistic and relentless foragers, covering up to 25 miles a day in search of food.
corrections.problem: No source supports 25 miles (40 km). The highest published figure is about 27 km/day (roughly 17 miles) for males and 10 km/day for females, from Kruuk & Mills (1983). Begg et al. (2003) go further and dispute the framing, finding both sexes forage over short distances when actually hunting, and that males' long-distance walking is mostly social (checking latrines, searching for females) and yields under 10% of their food intake.
corrections.suggestedFix: 'They are opportunistic and tireless foragers. Males can cover around 17 miles in a day and range over territories as large as 500 square kilometres, though much of that walking turns out to be social rather than hunting: checking scent latrines and looking for females. Females work a smaller patch more intensively, digging roughly ten holes per kilometre.'

corrections.claim: They are also remarkably fast and agile, able to climb trees and swim when needed.
corrections.problem: Climbing and swimming are well supported, but speed is directly contradicted. The Mammalian Species account states: 'Owing to the thickset form, stocky feet, and sharp and long foreclaws, honey badgers cannot run quickly. Their swinging trot or gallop is comparable with that of bears... The normal gait is a slow, rather bow-legged lumber, which they can maintain for hours.'
corrections.suggestedFix: 'They are not fast. Those long digging claws and stocky build give them a slow, bow-legged lumber, closer to a bear's gait than a weasel's. What they have instead is endurance, and they can keep that trot going for hours. They climb trees well enough to raid raptor nests and hives, and they swim well enough to chase turtles underwater.'

corrections.claim: Lions, leopards, and hyenas have all learned the hard way that getting a grip on a honey badger does not mean you have won the fight... A honey badger weighing 20 pounds will take on a lion... There are documented cases of honey badgers driving lions, leopards, and even small groups of wild dogs away from kills.
corrections.problem: Overstates the win rate and inverts the predator relationship. IUCN states plainly that 'Large carnivores such as Lion and Leopard prey on Honey Badger adults and cubs, while cubs are also killed by Black-backed Jackals.' Begg et al. (2005) recorded two incidents where a mother and cub were killed together by large predators, a young male's remains in a hyaena den, and 34% mean annual adult mortality. The Mammalian Species account describes a honey badger that fought a python for six hours and lost. On kill-stealing, IUCN supports only the generality that they 'may pirate food from other carnivores and will also scavenge from the kills of larger animals' - it names no species, and I found no primary documentation of honey badgers displacing lions, leopards or wild dog packs.
corrections.suggestedFix: Keep the toughness, drop the invincibility. Suggested: 'The loose hide genuinely does make a honey badger hard to hold, and they will pirate food from other carnivores and scavenge from bigger kills. But the internet version oversells it. Lions and leopards prey on honey badgers, adults included, and jackals take cubs. Field researchers in the Kalahari recorded two cases where a mother and her cub were killed together by large predators, found one young male's remains in a hyaena den, and measured adult annual mortality at 34%. One honey badger reportedly fought a python for six hours and lost. What is remarkable is not that they always win. It is that an animal this size makes the fight expensive enough that it is often not worth starting.'

corrections.claim: Researchers believe this resistance comes from genetic mutations in the honey badger's nicotinic acetylcholine receptors... [presented as explaining survival of both cobra and puff adder bites] ... After being bitten, a honey badger might collapse, go limp, and appear dead for a short time. Then it wakes up, shakes it off, and goes right back to eating the snake.
corrections.problem: Three issues. (1) The nAChR mutation described by Drabeck et al. (2015) blocks elapid alpha-neurotoxins - cobras and mambas. Puff adders are vipers with cytotoxic venom that works by a completely different mechanism, so this adaptation does not explain surviving puff adder bites, yet the article places both under one explanation. (2) The paper's convergence partners are hedgehogs and pigs; mongooses modify the same receptor by a different route (glycosylation), so 'the same type of adaptation seen in... mongooses' is loose. (3) The resistance was inferred from sequence analysis, not functionally tested, and is partial rather than absolute. On recovery: the Beggs' own record is a badger bitten in the face by a puff adder that 'showed signs of severe pain but recovered fully within five hours' - not a brief collapse shrugged off.
corrections.suggestedFix: 'Honey badgers survive snake bites that would kill a person, but the biology is more specific than the legend. A 2015 study found that honey badgers carry a mutation in the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, the exact molecular target of cobra and mamba neurotoxins. Swap in a positively charged amino acid and the toxin no longer docks properly. Hedgehogs and pigs evolved the same fix independently; mongooses reached a similar result by a different route. Two caveats matter. That mutation only defends against elapid neurotoxins, so it does not explain how honey badgers shrug off puff adders, which are vipers with cytotoxic venom that works on tissue rather than nerves. And the resistance is partial, not immunity: a big enough dose still kills. Recovery is also slower than the legend suggests. Researchers in the Kalahari watched a honey badger take a puff adder bite to the face. It was in obvious pain, and it took about five hours before it was fully back on its feet, swelling and all, hunting snakes again.'

corrections.claim: This kind of flexible, innovative problem-solving is associated with high cognitive ability... In captivity, they have been observed using tools, manipulating latches, and demonstrating what can only be described as a stubborn, creative intelligence.
corrections.problem: Presents an untested reputation as established science. There are no published studies of honey badger cognition at all. As Earth Touch reported, 'There are simply no studies of honey badger cognition anywhere in the scientific literature,' and the reputation 'is based solely on anecdote, not scientific study.' Cambridge primatologist William McGrew's reaction to the Stoffel footage was: 'Either honey badgers have been under-estimated, or this is a one-off genius honey badger, or it is a hoax,' and he called for actual problem-solving trials.
corrections.suggestedFix: Frame it honestly as an open question, which is more interesting anyway: 'Here is the strange part. Despite the reputation, nobody has ever run a proper study of honey badger cognition. Not one. Everything we think we know comes from anecdote and a handful of filmed escapes. Primatologist William McGrew, watching the Stoffel footage, summed up the problem: either honey badgers have been badly underestimated, or Stoffel was a one-off genius, or it is a hoax. He suggested someone go find out. What the field data do show is real if less cinematic. One Kalahari female invented her own springhare-hunting technique, tracking them by scent and cornering them underground, and her cub learned it and used it after leaving her. No other badger in the study bothered. Skills get invented, and passed on.'

corrections.claim: The skin is also tough enough to resist bee stings, porcupine quills, and even machete blows in some documented cases.
corrections.problem: The bee sting and quill claims trace to 19th and mid-20th century anecdote (Blumenbach 1825, Stevenson-Hamilton 1947, Rosevear 1974) rather than measurement, and the phrase 'documented cases' implies a rigor that does not exist. I could find no source of any kind for machete blows; that appears to be pure internet folklore.
corrections.suggestedFix: Cut the machete claim entirely and soften the rest: 'Naturalists have long reported that the hide turns bee stings, snake fangs and dog teeth, though these accounts are old and anecdotal rather than measured. What is documented is the thickness and the looseness, and those alone make a honey badger genuinely awkward to injure.'

corrections.claim: They are not currently considered endangered, though habitat loss and persecution by farmers (who view them as threats to livestock and beehives) do pose localized threats.
corrections.problem: Understates the situation and misorders the threats. The IUCN assessment does list Least Concern, but records 'Current Population Trend: Decreasing,' warns that 'clearly identifiable threats are operating, and known to be resulting in localised declines,' and notes 'evidence to suggest they have gone locally extinct in many areas through poisoning.' The dominant threat is direct persecution - steel-jaw traps and poison set by beekeepers and small-livestock farmers throughout the range, plus non-selective poisoning aimed at jackals and caracal - not habitat loss, which the article names first.
corrections.suggestedFix: 'The IUCN lists honey badgers as Least Concern, thanks to a huge range and a diet that adapts to almost anything. But the population trend is listed as decreasing, and the main pressure is not habitat loss. It is direct killing. Beekeepers and small-livestock farmers trap and poison them across their range, and honey badgers also die in non-selective poisoning campaigns aimed at jackals and caracal. Researchers believe they have gone locally extinct in many areas as a result.'

corrections.claim: Their jaws are strong enough to crush bone and even turtle shells.
corrections.problem: No published bite-force measurement exists for Mellivora capensis; the numbers circulating online trace only to content aggregators. The Mammalian Species account also describes a different mechanism for shells: 'carapaces of turtles... are peeled away to expose the softer inner parts,' meaning claws, not jaws.
corrections.suggestedFix: 'Nobody has actually measured a honey badger's bite force, so treat the numbers you see online with suspicion. What is described in the literature is a massive, wide-based skull with robust teeth, and a habit of peeling turtle carapaces open with those foreclaws rather than crushing them outright. The same technique works on hardened termite mounds, insect pupal cases and the clay capsules that lungfish seal themselves into.'

corrections.claim: Their digging aerates soil and creates burrows that other animals use. Their predation on snakes keeps populations in check.
corrections.problem: Both are plausible-sounding ecosystem claims with no supporting study. I found nothing documenting honey badgers as ecosystem engineers or quantifying secondary burrow use by other species, and no study testing whether their snake predation regulates snake populations. IUCN also notes honey badgers occur at low densities across most of their range (0.03 adults per square kilometre in the Kgalagadi), which makes strong top-down control of snake numbers unlikely.
corrections.suggestedFix: Either cut these two sentences or mark them as untested: 'They are also serious predators of snakes, which make up a large share of their diet by weight, though whether that meaningfully shapes snake populations has never been studied. Honey badgers live at low densities, roughly one adult per thirty square kilometres in the Kalahari, so their ecological footprint may be subtler than their reputation suggests.'

corrections.claim: Guinness World Records officially named it the world's most fearless animal.
corrections.problem: Minor, but the tense implies a live record. The title comes from the 2002 edition of the Guinness Book of World Records, per SANBI. It is not a currently listed Guinness record - there is no active entry on guinnessworldrecords.com.
corrections.suggestedFix: '...a reputation so wild that the 2002 Guinness Book of World Records named it the most fearless animal in the world.' Same effect, and it survives a fact-check.

claims.claim: Octopuses have three hearts: two branchial hearts push blood through the gills, and a systemic heart pumps oxygenated blood to the rest of the body.
claims.sourceCitation: Wells, M. J. (1980). Nervous control of the heartbeat in octopus. Journal of Experimental Biology, 85(1), 111-128. doi:10.1242/jeb.85.1.111
claims.note: Confirmed: the cephalopod circulatory system is 'based on a trio of hearts'; the paper works with 'the corresponding gill heart' and 'the systemic heart' as separate structures with separate cardiac ganglia.

claims.claim: When an octopus swims, the systemic heart actually stops beating.
claims.sourceCitation: Wells, M. J., Duthie, G. G., Houlihan, D. F., Smith, P. J. S., & Wells, J. (1987). Blood flow and pressure changes in exercising octopuses (Octopus vulgaris). Journal of Experimental Biology, 131(1), 175-187.
claims.note: The abstract states plainly: 'Jet propulsion is accompanied by cardiac arrest.' One narrowing worth making in the prose: this is documented for jet propulsion specifically, not for every mode of swimming.

claims.claim: The heart stops because the muscular effort of jet propulsion compresses the heart and disrupts its rhythm.
claims.sourceCitation: Wells, M. J., Duthie, G. G., Houlihan, D. F., Smith, P. J. S., & Wells, J. (1987). Blood flow and pressure changes in exercising octopuses (Octopus vulgaris). Journal of Experimental Biology, 131(1), 175-187.
claims.note: The mechanism is different. Wells et al. attribute the arrest to mantle pressure blocking venous return: 'the venous system is incapable of returning blood against the gradients produced by the rise in mean mantle pressure.' The heart stops because there is no blood arriving to pump, not because it is physically squeezed out of rhythm.

claims.claim: The resulting oxygen deficit is why octopuses prefer crawling to swimming.
claims.sourceCitation: Wells, M. J., Duthie, G. G., Houlihan, D. F., Smith, P. J. S., & Wells, J. (1987). Blood flow and pressure changes in exercising octopuses (Octopus vulgaris). Journal of Experimental Biology, 131(1), 175-187.
claims.note: The octopus can sustain an oxygen debt of only about 22 mL O2/kg, so 'jet-propelled movement is impossible for distances of more than a few metres.'

claims.claim: Octopus blood is blue because it uses copper-based hemocyanin instead of iron-based hemoglobin.
claims.sourceCitation: Oellermann, M., Lieb, B., Portner, H.-O., Semmens, J. M., & Mark, F. C. (2015). Blue blood on ice: modulated blood oxygen transport facilitates cold compensation and eurythermy in an Antarctic octopod. Frontiers in Zoology, 12:6. doi:10.1186/s12983-015-0097-x

claims.claim: Hemocyanin is less efficient than hemoglobin at body temperature but performs significantly better in cold, low-oxygen environments, exactly the deep chilly waters where many octopuses live.
claims.sourceCitation: Oellermann, M., Lieb, B., Portner, H.-O., Semmens, J. M., & Mark, F. C. (2015). Blue blood on ice: modulated blood oxygen transport facilitates cold compensation and eurythermy in an Antarctic octopod. Frontiers in Zoology, 12:6. doi:10.1186/s12983-015-0097-x
claims.note: This is backwards. Cold makes hemocyanin bind oxygen so tightly it cannot release it: at 0 C the Antarctic octopod Pareledone charcoti's hemocyanin would release 'only 16.3% of its bound oxygen,' whereas warming to 10 C lets it release 'most of the bound oxygen.' Cold is a problem the animal must compensate for, not an advantage. P. charcoti copes by carrying 40-46% more hemocyanin-bound oxygen than warmer-water relatives and by leaning on physically dissolved oxygen for 42% of tissue supply.

claims.claim: The skin contains three cell types working together: chromatophores (pigment sacs under muscular control), iridophores (structural light reflectors), and leucophores (broad light scatterers).
claims.sourceCitation: How, M. J., Norman, M. D., Finn, J., Chung, W.-S., & Marshall, N. J. (2017). Dynamic skin patterns in cephalopods. Frontiers in Physiology, 8:393. doi:10.3389/fphys.2017.00393
claims.note: Confirmed: chromatophores are 'elastic pigment-filled structures,' iridophores are 'wavelength interference platelet structures,' and leucophores provide a 'passive reflection component.'

claims.claim: Octopuses can change color and texture in milliseconds, and the entire transformation, color and texture together, can happen in under one second.
claims.sourceCitation: How, M. J., Norman, M. D., Finn, J., Chung, W.-S., & Marshall, N. J. (2017). Dynamic skin patterns in cephalopods. Frontiers in Physiology, 8:393. doi:10.3389/fphys.2017.00393
claims.note: The color half is roughly right but slower than 'milliseconds' implies: chromatic pulses in Octopus laqueus last 0.55 +/- 0.11 s, and the fastest component documented anywhere in the review is a cuttlefish hunting display element at '<0.25 s.' I found no measurement showing an octopus completing a combined color-plus-texture change in under one second.

claims.claim: Papillae are tiny muscular bumps that can be raised or flattened in fractions of a second.
claims.sourceCitation: Allen, J. J., Bell, G. R. R., Kuzirian, A. M., & Hanlon, R. T. (2013). Cuttlefish skin papilla morphology suggests a muscular hydrostatic function for rapid changeability. Journal of Morphology, 274(6), 645-656. doi:10.1002/jmor.20121
claims.note: Allen et al. establish the anatomy (concentric dermal erector muscles acting as a muscular hydrostat, built for 'rapid changeability') but deliberately do not quantify the speed. Widely repeated figures like 'one-fifth of a second' trace to press coverage, not to a number in this paper.

claims.claim: The mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus) was discovered off the coast of Indonesia in 1998.
claims.sourceCitation: Norman, M. D., Finn, J., & Tregenza, T. (2001). Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 268(1478), 1755-1758. doi:10.1098/rspb.2001.1708
claims.note: The 2001 paper places the work in Sulawesi and Bali and calls the animal 'new to science,' but gives no discovery year I could verify. Separately, the binomial is anachronistic in this sentence: Thaumoctopus mimicus was not erected until Norman & Hochberg (2005) in Molluscan Research, four years after the behavioral paper. Safest fix is 'first filmed by scientists off Indonesia in the late 1990s and formally named in 2005.'

claims.claim: The mimic octopus impersonates a venomous flatfish, a lionfish, and a banded sea snake.
claims.sourceCitation: Norman, M. D., Finn, J., & Tregenza, T. (2001). Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 268(1478), 1755-1758. doi:10.1098/rspb.2001.1708
claims.note: Nine individuals were observed 'displaying a repertoire of postures and body patterns, several of which are clearly impersonations of venomous animals co-occurring in this habitat.' The abstract does not name the three models individually; they are described in the body of the paper, which is the paper's entire subject.

claims.claim: Researchers believe the mimic octopus selects which animal to impersonate based on the specific predator it is trying to deter.
claims.sourceCitation: Norman, M. D., Finn, J., & Tregenza, T. (2001). Dynamic mimicry in an Indo-Malayan octopus. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 268(1478), 1755-1758. doi:10.1098/rspb.2001.1708
claims.note: Verbatim: 'our observations suggest that the octopus makes decisions about the most appropriate form of mimicry to use, allowing it to enhance further the benefits of mimicking toxic models by employing mimicry according to the nature of perceived threats.' The article's hedge ('Researchers believe') correctly matches the paper's own hedge; this rests on observation of nine animals, not an experiment.

claims.claim: The octopus nervous system has approximately 500 million neurons, comparable to a dog.
claims.sourceCitation: Carls-Diamante, S. (2022). Where is it like to be an octopus? Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 16:840022. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.840022
claims.note: Verbatim: 'With its 500 million neurons, a number more typical of vertebrates such as dogs, octopuses have the largest nervous systems among invertebrates.'

claims.claim: Roughly two-thirds of those neurons are not in the central brain but distributed through the eight arms.
claims.sourceCitation: Carls-Diamante, S. (2022). Where is it like to be an octopus? Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 16:840022. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.840022
claims.note: The figure is three-fifths (60%), not two-thirds: 'the arm nervous system contains three-fifths of the octopus's neurons,' with the brain itself 'the smallest component of the nervous system' at 45-50 million neurons. Godfrey-Smith independently describes 'nearly twice as many in total as in the central brain.' Close enough to keep, but 'roughly three-fifths' is the accurate word.

claims.claim: They have nine brains: one central brain and one mini-brain in each of their eight arms.
claims.sourceCitation: Carls-Diamante, S. (2022). Where is it like to be an octopus? Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 16:840022. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.840022
claims.note: An octopus has one brain (45-50 million neurons) plus an arm nervous system of axial nerve cords and ganglia. The arms are not brains and no source in the peer-reviewed literature describes them as such. 'Nine brains' is popular shorthand that this site's primary-source standard should not repeat as anatomy.

claims.claim: A severed octopus arm can still respond to stimuli and attempt to pass food toward where the mouth used to be.
claims.sourceCitation: Carls-Diamante, S. (2022). Where is it like to be an octopus? Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 16:840022. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.840022
claims.note: The reflex half is well documented: 'when pricked, a freshly amputated arm would demonstrate a number of responses identical to those found in intact animals,' with grasping persisting 'up to three hours after the arm had been amputated.' Godfrey-Smith adds reaching and grasping. The specific detail about passing food toward the absent mouth is reported elsewhere but I could not verify it from any source I opened.

claims.claim: Arm movement and sensory processing are handled largely by the arms themselves rather than by central command.
claims.sourceCitation: Hochner, B. (2012). An embodied view of octopus neurobiology. Current Biology, 22(20), R887-R892. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2012.09.001
claims.note: Hochner frames the eight flexible arms as posing 'a great challenge' precisely because of 'the infinite degrees of freedom that have to be controlled' and because 'it is hard to use body coordinates in this flexible animal to represent sensory information in a central control system' - which is why control is pushed to the periphery.

claims.claim: Octopuses in laboratory settings have learned to open childproof jars to retrieve food inside.
claims.sourceCitation: Richter, J. N., Hochner, B., & Kuba, M. J. (2016). Pull or push? Octopuses solve a puzzle problem. PLoS ONE, 11(3), e0152048. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0152048
claims.note: The published record covers jars 'closed by a rubber plug' (Fiorito et al.), L-shaped puzzle containers (Richter et al.), and screw-on test tube caps (Jarmoluk & Pelled 2025). 'Childproof' is a popular embellishment I could find in no peer-reviewed source.

claims.claim: They navigate complex mazes, remember the correct route, and improve their performance over repeated trials.
claims.sourceCitation: Richter, J. N., Hochner, B., & Kuba, M. J. (2016). Pull or push? Octopuses solve a puzzle problem. PLoS ONE, 11(3), e0152048. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0152048
claims.note: The learning half is solidly supported: all seven octopuses solved a five-level container task, and 'at the onset of each new level the performance of the animals dropped... However, they adapted quickly.' The maze claim is a different experimental paradigm and I could not verify it from any source I opened. Octopus maze literature does exist, so this is a sourcing gap rather than a known error.

claims.claim: They recognize individual human faces.
claims.sourceCitation: Anderson, R. C., Mather, J. A., Monette, M. Q., & Zimsen, S. R. M. (2010). Octopuses (Enteroctopus dofleini) recognize individual humans. Journal of Applied Animal Welfare Science, 13(3), 261-272. doi:10.1080/10888705.2010.483892
claims.note: The study is 'recognize individual humans,' not faces. Eight octopuses were exposed for two weeks to one person who fed them and one who touched them with a bristly stick; they then differed significantly in eyebar body pattern, arm reaching, funnel direction and (in the four larger animals) respiration rate. Nothing in the design isolates facial features from body, motion, or other visual cues.

claims.claim: One octopus at a New Zealand aquarium was notorious for squirting water at a particular staff member.
claims.sourceCitation: Godfrey-Smith, P. (2017). The Mind of an Octopus. Scientific American Mind, 28(1), 62.
claims.note: It was a university laboratory, not an aquarium: 'At the University of Otago in New Zealand, this game became so expensive that the octopus had to be released back to the wild.' The animal 'took a dislike to one member of the staff, for no obvious reason' and delivered 'a half-gallon jet of water down the back of her neck.' This is an anecdote reported by a philosopher of science, not a study.

claims.claim: Veined octopuses (Amphioctopus marginatus) collect discarded coconut shell halves, carry them considerable distances, and assemble them into a portable shelter.
claims.sourceCitation: Finn, J. K., Tregenza, T., & Norman, M. D. (2009). Defensive tool use in a coconut-carrying octopus. Current Biology, 19(23), R1069-R1070. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2009.10.052
claims.note: Citation confirmed on PubMed, which lists it as a Letter with no abstract; the publisher full text is paywalled. The study rests on more than 500 diver hours off Northern Sulawesi and Bali (1999-2008) and over 20 individuals, with four observed carrying stacked shells up to 20 m.

claims.claim: The octopus carries the shells even when they are not immediately useful, suggesting it is planning for future use.
claims.sourceCitation: Finn, J. K., Tregenza, T., & Norman, M. D. (2009). Defensive tool use in a coconut-carrying octopus. Current Biology, 19(23), R1069-R1070. doi:10.1016/j.cub.2009.10.052
claims.note: This deferred benefit is the paper's entire argument for calling the behavior tool use: while carried the shells 'offer no protection' and force a cumbersome 'stilt-walking' gait. Worth presenting as the authors' interpretation rather than settled fact.

claims.claim: Researchers have documented play behavior in octopuses.
claims.sourceCitation: Jarmoluk, K., & Pelled, G. (2025). Evidence of play behavior in captive California two-spot octopuses, Octopus bimaculoides. PLOS ONE, 20(7), e0326379. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0326379
claims.note: Three of nine octopuses learned to unscrew test tube caps and repeatedly performed release-grasp sequences meeting established play criteria. The paper also confirms the article's framing that play 'engage[s] neurobiological mechanisms that support learning, memory, and the development of flexible behavioral strategies.'

claims.claim: Individual octopuses in captivity have distinct personalities: bold and exploratory versus shy and cautious.
claims.sourceCitation: Jarmoluk, K., & Pelled, G. (2025). Evidence of play behavior in captive California two-spot octopuses, Octopus bimaculoides. PLOS ONE, 20(7), e0326379. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0326379
claims.note: Jarmoluk & Pelled cite individual personality differences in octopuses and note that 'personality traits may influence the likelihood of an octopus to engage in play activity.' The originating primary source is Mather & Anderson (1993), J. Comp. Psychol. 107(3):336-340, which isolated three dimensions (Activity, Reactivity, Avoidance) across 44 Octopus rubescens; I could not open that paper (paywalled), so it is not in the sources block.

claims.claim: Octopuses are widely considered the most intelligent invertebrates on Earth.
claims.sourceCitation: Carls-Diamante, S. (2022). Where is it like to be an octopus? Frontiers in Systems Neuroscience, 16:840022. doi:10.3389/fnsys.2022.840022
claims.note: 'Most intelligent' is a judgment rather than a measurement, but the neural anchor holds: 'octopuses have the largest nervous systems among invertebrates.'

claims.claim: They can taste with their suckers, which are lined with chemoreceptors that detect flavor and texture simultaneously.
claims.sourceCitation: van Giesen, L., Kilian, P. B., Allard, C. A. H., & Bellono, N. W. (2020). Molecular basis of chemotactile sensation in octopus. Cell, 183(3), 594-604.e14. doi:10.1016/j.cell.2020.09.008
claims.note: The 'taste by touch' framing is exactly right, but the mechanism is misattributed. Chemical and mechanical signals are handled by two separate cell populations, not by chemoreceptors doing both: 'distinct chemo- and mechanosensory cells exhibit specific receptor expression and electrical activities.' Chemotactile receptors respond to terpenoids; touch runs through a NompC-type mechanoreceptor.

claims.claim: Most octopus species survive only one to two years.
claims.sourceCitation: Grearson, A. G., et al. (2021). The lesser Pacific striped octopus, Octopus chierchiae: an emerging laboratory model. Frontiers in Marine Science, 8:753483. doi:10.3389/fmars.2021.753483
claims.note: Supported indirectly: O. chierchiae 'may regularly live for up to 2 years' and this is 'a comparable, if not longer, lifespan than many other octopus species commonly reared in culture.'

claims.claim: Octopuses are semelparous, meaning they reproduce once and then die.
claims.sourceCitation: Grearson, A. G., et al. (2021). The lesser Pacific striped octopus, Octopus chierchiae: an emerging laboratory model. Frontiers in Marine Science, 8:753483. doi:10.3389/fmars.2021.753483
claims.note: True of most species, not all. The paper is explicit both ways: 'Most octopus species are semelparous and die after one reproductive event,' but 'Unlike most octopus species, O. chierchiae is iteroparous,' laying successive clutches roughly every 30-90 days.

claims.claim: After mating, the male wanders off and dies within weeks.
claims.sourceCitation: Alaska Department of Fish and Game. Giant Pacific Octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) Species Profile.
claims.note: Confirmed for the giant Pacific octopus: after passing the spermatophore, 'he dies a few weeks later.' Verified for this species specifically rather than octopuses generally.

claims.claim: The female stops eating, aerates and guards her eggs continuously, and dies shortly after they hatch.
claims.sourceCitation: Wang, Z. Y., & Ragsdale, C. W. (2018). Multiple optic gland signaling pathways implicated in octopus maternal behaviors and death. Journal of Experimental Biology, 221(19), jeb185751. doi:10.1242/jeb.185751
claims.note: Supported in outline: 'the mother cares for her clutch of eggs without feeding until her death.' One nuance the article misses: fasting is not immediate. Wang & Ragsdale document a 'feeding brooding' stage of about 8 +/- 2.71 days before an 11 +/- 8.49 day fasting stage and then a distinct decline stage. Corroborated by the Monterey Bay Aquarium ('She doesn't eat during this time, and usually dies shortly after the young hatch').

claims.claim: The giant Pacific octopus is the largest of all octopus species and lives perhaps three to five years.
claims.sourceCitation: Monterey Bay Aquarium. Giant Pacific Octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini).
claims.note: Both figures confirmed twice over. Monterey Bay: 'the largest octopus in the world,' lifespan 'about three to five years,' arm span often exceeding 13 feet. Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game: 'the largest octopus species in the world,' 'The lifespan of E. dofleini is thought to be 3-to-5-years.'

claims.claim: Female giant Pacific octopuses can lay up to 100,000 eggs in a single clutch.
claims.sourceCitation: Alaska Department of Fish and Game. Giant Pacific Octopus (Enteroctopus dofleini) Species Profile.
claims.note: ADF&G: females 'lay up to 100,000 eggs in long strands.' Monterey Bay gives the fuller distribution: '18,000 to 74,000 eggs (occasionally up to 100,000).' 100,000 is the ceiling, not the norm, and the article's 'up to' phrasing handles that correctly.

claims.claim: Octopus ink contains tyrosinase, which dulls a predator's sense of smell and buys the octopus time to escape.
claims.sourceCitation: Derby, C. D. (2014). Cephalopod ink: production, chemistry, functions and applications. Marine Drugs, 12(5), 2700-2730. doi:10.3390/md12052700
claims.note: The definitive review kills this one. Ink 'has been proposed as an aversive deterrent or as a disruptor of predators' chemical senses,' but Derby immediately adds: 'To date, there are no reports of experimental tests of cephalopod ink as an inactivator or disruptor of the chemical senses.' The only tyrosinase-linked predator effect discussed is speculation that quinones produced via tyrosinase might act as feeding deterrents, which concerns taste and palatability, not smell. Tyrosinase is genuinely present in ink; the smell-dulling function is not established.

claims.claim: The blue-ringed octopus's tetrodotoxin can kill a human within minutes and has no known antidote.
claims.sourceCitation: Divers Alert Network. Blue-Ringed Octopus (health resource page).
claims.note: 'No antidote' is correct: 'There is no antivenom available,' and treatment is 'symptomatic and supportive.' 'Within minutes' is not. Symptoms start within minutes, but 'Death may occur as early as 20 minutes or as late as 24 hours after exposure; it usually occurs within the first 4 to 8 hours.' The lethal dose figure (about half a milligram for an adult) and TTX's potency relative to cyanide are both confirmed.

claims.claim: The Kraken of Norse mythology was almost certainly inspired by encounters with giant squid and octopuses.
claims.sourceCitation: Salvador, R. B., & Tomotani, B. M. (2014). The Kraken: when myth encounters science. Historia, Ciencias, Saude-Manguinhos, 21(3), 971-994. doi:10.1590/S0104-59702014000300010
claims.note: The scholarship points at squid only: 'Today we know the legends of this monster were based on sightings of giant squids.' The paper traces the identification to Steenstrup's 1853 description of Architeuthis dux and notes that even sea serpent legends resolve to Architeuthis. Octopuses are not implicated. Since this is an octopus article, the 'and octopuses' is the tempting addition to make and the one the source does not support.

claims.claim: The octopus has no skeleton and can squeeze through any opening large enough to fit its beak, the only hard part of its body.
claims.sourceCitation: Malik, W. (2016, April 14). Inky's Daring Escape Shows How Smart Octopuses Are. National Geographic.
claims.note: The soft-body half is uncontroversial: octopuses 'can squeeze through small openings because of their soft, boneless bodies.' The specific beak-as-limiting-aperture rule is repeated everywhere in popular writing and I could find no primary source that tests or quantifies it. The chitin composition of the beak is likewise unsourced here. Recommend softening to the boneless-body claim unless a primary source turns up.

claims.claim: Octopuses are escape artists that slip out of tanks, cross the floor, and find their way back to the ocean.
claims.sourceCitation: Malik, W. (2016, April 14). Inky's Daring Escape Shows How Smart Octopuses Are. National Geographic.
claims.note: Inky escaped the National Aquarium of New Zealand in 2016 by moving his tank lid, sliding across the floor at night, and squeezing through a drainpipe leading to open water. Worth noting that Inky was never recovered, so reaching the sea is inferred from the trail and the pipe's outlet, not confirmed.

claims.claim: Octopuses collect and carefully arrange rocks outside their dens, a behavior resembling decorating a home.
claims.note: I could not open a primary source. The originating study is almost certainly Mather, J. A. (1994), 'Home' choice and modification by juvenile Octopus vulgaris (Mollusca: Cephalopoda): specialized intelligence and tool use?, Journal of Zoology 233:359-368, which reports juveniles selecting den sites and modifying them by removing rocks and sand and bringing in items to partly block the aperture. That is functional den modification rather than decoration, so the 'decorating a home' framing likely overstates it even if the underlying behavior checks out.

claims.claim: The octopus's last common ancestor with vertebrates was a simple flatworm-like creature.
claims.note: I could not verify this from any source I opened; the relevant review (Roth, G. 2015, Convergent evolution of complex brains and high intelligence, Phil. Trans. R. Soc. B 370:20150049) was blocked at the publisher. Divergence estimates in the 550-600 million year range and an early bilaterian ancestor are widely cited, but 'flatworm-like' is a specific morphological claim about an unfossilized ancestor. Recommend softening to 'an early bilaterian ancestor more than half a billion years ago.'

claims.claim: The 2020 Netflix documentary 'My Octopus Teacher,' documenting Craig Foster's year with a wild octopus in a South African kelp forest, won an Academy Award.
claims.sourceCitation: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences / ABC. My Octopus Teacher is the 2021 Oscar Winner for Documentary (Feature). 93rd Academy Awards, April 25, 2021.
claims.note: Confirmed: released on Netflix September 7, 2020, filmed in a kelp forest in False Bay near Cape Town, directed by Pippa Ehrlich and James Reed, and awarded Documentary (Feature) at the 93rd Academy Awards on April 25, 2021.

claims.claim: The octopus has a brain that wraps around its throat.
claims.note: Not checked against a primary source. The octopus brain is a ring of fused ganglia around the esophagus, so this is very likely correct, but it is a specific anatomical claim and should carry a citation before publication under a primary-source standard.

corrections.claim: Hemocyanin is actually less efficient than hemoglobin at body temperature, but it has a crucial advantage: it performs significantly better in cold, low-oxygen environments, exactly the kind of deep, chilly ocean waters where many octopus species live.
corrections.problem: This is backwards, and it is the most serious error in the article. Cold does not help hemocyanin, it cripples it. Oellermann et al. (2015) measured that at 0 C the Antarctic octopod Pareledone charcoti's hemocyanin would release 'only 16.3% of its bound oxygen' under normal arterial-venous conditions, while warming to 10 C lets it release 'most of the bound oxygen.' Cold-water octopuses succeed despite hemocyanin, not because of it: P. charcoti carries 40-46% more hemocyanin-bound oxygen than warmer-water relatives, and physically dissolved oxygen supplies another 42% of what reaches the tissues.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Hemocyanin is less efficient than hemoglobin at carrying oxygen, and cold water makes the problem worse rather than better. In near-freezing seas, hemocyanin grips oxygen so tightly it struggles to hand it over: researchers measured an Antarctic octopus releasing only about 16 percent of its bound oxygen at 0 C, against most of it at 10 C. Cold-water octopuses get around this by flooding their blood with extra hemocyanin, up to 46 percent more than warmer-water relatives, and by leaning on the oxygen that dissolves directly into cold seawater. Evolution did not hand the octopus a better molecule. It handed it a workable one and let the animal compensate.'

corrections.claim: When an octopus inks, the cloud does more than obscure vision: it also contains a compound called tyrosinase that dulls a predator's sense of smell, giving the octopus extra time to escape.
corrections.problem: The definitive review of cephalopod ink chemistry says this has never been tested. Derby (2014) notes ink 'has been proposed as an aversive deterrent or as a disruptor of predators' chemical senses,' then states flatly: 'To date, there are no reports of experimental tests of cephalopod ink as an inactivator or disruptor of the chemical senses.' The only tyrosinase-linked predator effect he discusses is speculation that quinones might deter feeding, which is about taste, not smell. Tyrosinase is really in the ink; the smell-dulling job is folklore.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Octopus ink is chemically busy in ways that go beyond the smokescreen. It carries dopa, dopamine, melanin and the enzyme tyrosinase, and researchers have long suspected the mix interferes with a predator's chemical senses as well as its vision. Suspected, not shown: as of the most recent major review, no one has actually run the experiment.'

corrections.claim: They have nine brains: one central brain and one mini-brain in each of their eight arms, allowing each arm to act semi-independently.
corrections.problem: The arms contain nerve cords and ganglia, not brains. Carls-Diamante (2022) describes a single brain of 45-50 million neurons, which is 'the smallest component of the nervous system,' alongside an arm nervous system holding three-fifths of the animal's neurons. No peer-reviewed source calls the arms brains. On a site that runs a primary-source standard, this is the kind of shorthand that should not survive.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Their nervous system is radically decentralized. One brain sits between the eyes, but it holds only about 45 to 50 million of the animal's neurons, and three-fifths of the total run down the eight arms in their own nerve cords. Each arm can sense, decide and move with startling independence, which is where the popular line about nine brains comes from. It is one brain and eight remarkably opinionated limbs.'

corrections.claim: They recognize individual human faces and have been documented behaving differently toward researchers they like versus those they find annoying (one octopus at a New Zealand aquarium was notorious for squirting water at a particular staff member).
corrections.problem: Two errors in one sentence. First, the study is titled 'Octopuses recognize individual humans,' not faces: Anderson et al. (2010) had one person feed eight octopuses and another touch them with a bristly stick for two weeks, then measured differences in eyebar pattern, arm reaching, funnel direction and respiration. Nothing isolates facial features from body shape, movement or other cues. Second, the water-squirting octopus was at the University of Otago, a research laboratory, not an aquarium, and it comes from Godfrey-Smith's anecdote rather than a study.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'They tell individual people apart. In one study, eight giant Pacific octopuses spent two weeks with two humans, one who fed them and one who prodded them with a bristly stick, and by the end they responded differently to each: different skin patterns, different arm movements, different breathing rates. The lab stories are better still. At the University of Otago in New Zealand, one octopus took a dislike to a particular staff member and delivered half a gallon of water down the back of her neck every time she walked past, until the animal had to be released back to the wild.'

corrections.claim: Octopuses in laboratory settings have learned to open childproof jars to retrieve food inside.
corrections.problem: 'Childproof' appears nowhere in the peer-reviewed record. What is actually published: jars sealed with rubber plugs (Fiorito et al.), five-level L-shaped puzzle containers (Richter, Hochner & Kuba 2016), and screw-on test tube caps (Jarmoluk & Pelled 2025). The real results are impressive enough without the upgrade.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Octopuses in the lab work open sealed containers to get at food: glass jars stoppered with plugs, screw-top test tubes, and multi-stage puzzle boxes that have to be levered through a tight opening in a particular orientation. In one study all seven animals solved a five-level version of the task, and although their performance dipped each time the rules changed, they adapted quickly.'

corrections.claim: Some octopus species are venomous, and the blue-ringed octopus is among the most venomous animals on Earth: its venom contains tetrodotoxin, which can kill a human within minutes and has no known antidote.
corrections.problem: 'No antidote' is correct. 'Kill within minutes' is not. Per Divers Alert Network, symptoms start within minutes, but 'Death may occur as early as 20 minutes or as late as 24 hours after exposure; it usually occurs within the first 4 to 8 hours.' The distinction matters practically: the window is long enough that ventilatory support saves people, which is exactly why the absence of an antivenom is survivable.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Some octopus species are venomous, and the blue-ringed octopus is among the most dangerous animals in the ocean. Its venom contains tetrodotoxin, roughly half a milligram of which can kill an adult, and there is no antivenom. Symptoms set in within minutes, though death, when it comes, usually takes four to eight hours. Because the toxin kills by paralyzing the muscles used to breathe, victims who reach a ventilator in time generally recover fully.'

corrections.claim: The Kraken of Norse mythology, a sea monster large enough to drag entire ships beneath the waves, was almost certainly inspired by encounters with giant squid and octopuses.
corrections.problem: The scholarship credits squid alone. Salvador & Tomotani (2014) state: 'Today we know the legends of this monster were based on sightings of giant squids,' tracing the identification to Steenstrup's 1853 description of Architeuthis dux, and note that even sea serpent legends resolve to the same animal. Octopuses are not implicated. This is the natural embellishment to make in an octopus article and the one the source rules out.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'The Kraken of Norse legend, a sea monster large enough to drag entire ships under, is now generally credited to sightings of the giant squid, formally described as Architeuthis dux in 1853 from a carcass that washed up on a Danish beach.' Then add a beat acknowledging the octopus was written into the myth later, rather than claiming it was there at the start.

corrections.claim: Octopuses are semelparous, meaning they reproduce once and then die.
corrections.problem: True of most species, but stated as universal. Grearson et al. (2021) put both halves plainly: 'Most octopus species are semelparous and die after one reproductive event,' but 'Unlike most octopus species, O. chierchiae is iteroparous,' laying successive clutches roughly every 30 to 90 days and living up to two years while staying fertile.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'Most octopuses are semelparous, meaning they reproduce once and then die.' Optionally add: 'There are exceptions. The lesser Pacific striped octopus lays clutch after clutch, every 30 to 90 days, and stays fertile for most of its adult life.'

corrections.claim: This is because the muscular effort of jet propulsion (the octopus forces water through a siphon to move) compresses the heart and disrupts its rhythm.
corrections.problem: The heart stopping is real, the explanation is not. Wells et al. (1987) attribute the arrest to blocked venous return, not mechanical compression: 'the venous system is incapable of returning blood against the gradients produced by the rise in mean mantle pressure.' Pressure inside the mantle rises high enough that blood cannot get back to the heart, so the heart has nothing to pump.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'The reason is plumbing rather than muscle strain. Jetting spikes the pressure inside the mantle so high that blood in the veins cannot flow back against it. With nothing arriving to pump, the systemic heart simply stops. The octopus can only run up an oxygen debt of about 22 millilitres per kilogram, which is why jet propulsion is impossible for more than a few metres at a stretch.'

corrections.claim: They can change color and texture in milliseconds using chromatophores. ... The entire transformation, color and texture together, can happen in under one second.
corrections.problem: The measured numbers are slower. How et al. (2017) clock chromatic pulses in Octopus laqueus at 0.55 +/- 0.11 seconds, and the fastest single component reported anywhere in that review is a cuttlefish hunting display element at under 0.25 seconds. No published measurement shows an octopus completing a combined color-and-texture change in under a second, and Allen et al. (2013) deliberately decline to put a number on papilla speed at all.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace both instances with: 'They can flush a new color across the skin in well under a second, with individual chromatic pulses measured at roughly half a second.' For the texture sentence: 'Texture changes are slower than color changes, and no one has yet published a precise figure for how fast an octopus can raise or flatten its papillae, but the anatomy, a muscular hydrostat of concentric erector muscles, is clearly built for speed.'

corrections.claim: They can taste with their suckers, which are lined with chemoreceptors that detect flavor and texture simultaneously.
corrections.problem: The 'taste by touch' idea is right, the mechanism is misassigned. van Giesen et al. (2020) found two separate cell populations, not one dual-purpose receptor: 'distinct chemo- and mechanosensory cells exhibit specific receptor expression and electrical activities.' Chemotactile receptors respond to terpenoids; touch runs through a separate NompC-type mechanoreceptor.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'They taste by touch. Each sucker carries two separate populations of sensory cells, one tuned to chemistry and one to touch, so an arm reaching blindly into a crevice reads flavor and texture at the same instant without waiting on the brain.'

corrections.claim: The female finds a den, lays her eggs (sometimes tens of thousands of them), and then dedicates the remainder of her life entirely to their care. She stops eating.
corrections.problem: Fasting is not immediate, and the real sequence is more interesting than the myth. Wang & Ragsdale (2018) documented four distinct stages: a 'feeding brooding' phase of about 8 days where she tends the clutch and still eats, then roughly 11 days of fasting while guarding, then a decline phase marked by 'retraction of the skin around the eyes, general paling of skin color, and loss of motor tone,' self-grooming to the point of injury, and occasional self-cannibalization.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'She lays her eggs, sometimes tens of thousands of them, and settles in. For the first week or so she still eats while tending the clutch. Then she stops, and does not start again. She spends the following weeks aerating the eggs with her siphon and guarding them without rest, and researchers who have tracked the decline describe the final stage in unsparing detail: the skin around her eyes retracts, her color fades, her muscle tone goes. By the time the eggs hatch she is dying.'

corrections.claim: the mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus), discovered off the coast of Indonesia in 1998
corrections.problem: The name is anachronistic and the date is unsourced. Norman, Finn & Tregenza (2001) describe the animal as 'new to science' from dives in Sulawesi and Bali but give no discovery year I could verify from the paper. The binomial Thaumoctopus mimicus was not erected until Norman & Hochberg published the formal description in Molluscan Research in 2005, four years after the behavior paper.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'the mimic octopus (Thaumoctopus mimicus), first filmed by scientists off Sulawesi and Bali in the late 1990s, described in the literature in 2001 and formally named in 2005'
