claims.claim: An animal the size of a medium dog that will aggressively defend a carcass against animals many times its size, drag a full-grown caribou through deep snow, and range hundreds of miles without rest.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine. National Park Service species article (nps.gov/articles/wolverine.htm)
claims.note: NPS confirms wolverines are "capable of capturing and killing prey that is much larger than themselves such as a moose or caribou," but ADF&G's species profile says killing large prey is rare, and NPS says that "more often than killing, wolverines will scavenge carcasses of animals killed by other predators, drag them away from the kill sites, and cache them." Nothing in the literature documents a wolverine dragging an intact adult caribou. What is documented is dragging portions of carcasses away to cache them.

claims.claim: The wolverine (Gulo gulo) is the largest land-dwelling member of the weasel family.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine Species Profile. Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: ADF&G: "the largest terrestrial member of the family Mustelidae." The Wolverine Foundation states the same. The qualifier "land-dwelling" is doing correct work here, since sea otters and giant otters are heavier.

claims.claim: It rarely weighs more than 40 pounds.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine Species Profile. Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: ADF&G: adult males "generally weigh 24-40 pounds (11-18 kg)" and adult females 13-26 pounds. ADF&G biologist Howard Golden: "A big wolverine is 40 pounds."

claims.claim: Wolverines have been documented displacing cougars from their kills (stated twice in the body, and again in the excerpt and meta description).
claims.sourceCitation: Gulo gulo (wolverine). Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology
claims.note: This is the article's single most repeated claim and I could not find a primary source for it. Animal Diversity Web says wolverines "have been reported to drive bears, cougars, and even packs of wolves from their kills" but gives no citation for it, and that uncited sentence appears to be the origin of the claim across the popular web. Searches of the puma kill-site literature turned up nothing: Allen et al. 2014 (PLOS ONE 9:e102257) camera-monitored 58 puma kills and logged 20 scavenger species with no wolverine, and Elbroch & Wittmer 2012 (Biol. Lett. 8:776-779) does not mention wolverines. Bell et al. 2023 (Sci. Rep. 13:11026) found wolverines reduced their scavenging rate in lynx high-use areas, i.e. fine-scale avoidance of a competitor, not dominance. ADF&G states flatly that wolverines "will not attack a larger predator, like a wolf or a bear."

claims.claim: Wolves and bears are genuine predators of wolverines.
claims.sourceCitation: Young, K.B., Saalfeld, D.T., Brandt, C., Smith, K.R., Spivey, T.J. & Stantorf, C.J. (2023). Interspecific killing of wolverines by one wolf pack. Ecology and Evolution 13(12):e10758. doi:10.1002/ece3.10758
claims.note: Necropsies showed puncture wounds in hide and skull indicative of wolves, and the wolverines were not consumed, so this was competitive killing rather than predation for food. ADF&G separately notes that encounters with wolves and bears "may be fatal to the wolverine."

claims.claim: Alaska Dept. of Fish and Game reports that researchers have never observed a wolverine chase off a bear.
claims.sourceCitation: Woodford, R. (2014). Wolverines: Behind the Myth. Alaska Fish and Wildlife News, Alaska Department of Fish and Game, December 2014
claims.note: Accurate in substance, slightly loose in attribution. It is a direct quote from ADF&G biologist Howard Golden: "You hear stories about them chasing bears off, I've never seen that happen, or known anyone who has." That is one biologist's testimony in an agency magazine, not a formal agency finding. Wording it as "an ADF&G biologist says" would be more precise.

claims.claim: A 2023 study in Ecology and Evolution found a single wolf pack killed three of four collared wolverines in Alaska.
claims.sourceCitation: Young, K.B., Saalfeld, D.T., Brandt, C., Smith, K.R., Spivey, T.J. & Stantorf, C.J. (2023). Interspecific killing of wolverines by one wolf pack. Ecology and Evolution 13(12):e10758. doi:10.1002/ece3.10758
claims.note: Exactly right. Four wolverines collared in Chugach State Park and Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson near Anchorage between 4 Jan 2022 and 16 Apr 2023; three killed by members of one collared wolf pack (Wolverines 2, 7 and 6), one (Wolverine 5) survived.

claims.claim: Their jaws are powerful enough to crush frozen bone.
claims.sourceCitation: Woodford, R. (2014). Wolverines: Behind the Myth. Alaska Fish and Wildlife News, Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: ADF&G biologist Howard Golden: "They've got incredibly strong jaws for biting and crushing bone and frozen meat, not the same crushing power as a wolf, but they're not as big." The comparative caveat is worth keeping in mind if the article ever escalates this.

claims.claim: A single male wolverine can patrol a home range of up to 240 square miles.
claims.sourceCitation: Persson, J., Wedholm, P. & Segerström, P. (2010). Space use and territoriality of wolverines (Gulo gulo) in northern Scandinavia. European Journal of Wildlife Research 56:49-57. doi:10.1007/s10344-009-0290-3
claims.note: If anything conservative. Persson et al. found male mean home range 669 km2 (258 sq mi); ADF&G gives Alaska resident males 200-260 sq mi in the species profile and 270-380 sq mi in Behind the Myth; NPS Yellowstone reports 350 sq mi (908 km2) for males; The Wolverine Foundation cites a 422-1,506 km2 range across studies. The figure is fine but "up to" understates the upper end.

claims.claim: One of the largest territories of any land mammal relative to body size.
claims.sourceCitation: Stinson, D. et al. (2013). Wolverine (Gulo gulo). Encyclopedia of Puget Sound / Washington Department of Fish and Wildlife
claims.note: The underlying observation is real: Inman et al. 2012 (J. Wildl. Manage. 76:778-792) recorded GYE home ranges of 303 km2 for females and 797 km2 for males and described them as large relative to body size. But no source I found ranks the wolverine against all land mammals on that metric, so the superlative is unsupported as written.

claims.claim: They mark every inch of that range with a pungent musk secreted from glands near the base of the tail.
claims.sourceCitation: General Wolverine Characteristics. The Wolverine Foundation
claims.note: Wrong mechanism. The Wolverine Foundation: "Although wolverines have well developed anal musk glands, musking appears to be used primarily as a fear-defense mechanism" and "chemical communication is accomplished via scentmarking with urine and abdominal rubbing." ADF&G's Behind the Myth lists three gland sets: "a ventral gland near the belly button, anal glands, and they also have little scent glands on the bottom of the pads of their feet." So the anal glands near the tail base are the defensive ones, and routine territorial marking is mostly urine plus belly rubbing.

claims.claim: This scent-marking system is so effective that other wolverines, predators, and even experienced trappers can detect it from a considerable distance.
claims.sourceCitation: Wood, W.F., Terwilliger, M.N. & Copeland, J.P. (2005). Volatile compounds from anal glands of the wolverine, Gulo gulo. Journal of Chemical Ecology 31(9):2111-2117. doi:10.1007/s10886-005-6080-9
claims.note: The one chemical analysis of wolverine anal gland secretion found that "the pungent thietanes and dithiolanes found in other mustelids were absent." The dominant compounds were short-chain fatty acids, phenylacetic acid, alpha-tocopherol and cholesterol. In other words wolverine musk is notably less pungent than that of skunks, mink and weasels, which is the opposite of what the sentence implies. The "trappers can smell it from a distance" detail has no source at all.

claims.claim: Wolverines can smell prey buried under up to 20 feet of snow. That is not a typo.
claims.sourceCitation: Woodford, R. (2014). Wolverines: Behind the Myth. Alaska Fish and Wildlife News, Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: No primary source exists for the 20 foot figure. It traces to a PBS Nature web page for the film Wolverine: Chasing the Phantom (pbs.org, 2010), which asserts it without citation, and every popular repetition traces back there. A USDA Forest Service Science Findings piece gives 6 feet instead, and other popular sources give 2 metres, so the number is not even stable. The defensible version is ADF&G biologist Howard Golden's: "a really good nose, they can smell food over long distances or buried well under the snow," with no depth attached. Note also that the paragraph slides from smelling prey to excavating carcasses, and 20 feet of settled snowpack is deeper than almost any documented wolverine dig.

claims.claim: The fur is uniquely structured to resist frost and moisture; ice and snow do not cling to it the way they do to other animal coats. Indigenous peoples of the Arctic have long prized wolverine fur for lining the hoods of parkas for exactly this reason.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine Species Profile (printer edition). Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: The outcome and the cultural use are solid: ADF&G says the fur "is commonly used for parka trim and hoods because of its beauty and durability and because the guard hairs of wolverine fur resist frost accumulation," and Animal Diversity Web notes native peoples used wolverine pelts to line parkas. The mechanism claim is where it drifts. Frost does form on wolverine fur; what is unusual is how easily it brushes off, and no published work has identified why. Scanning electron microscopy work has specifically ruled out the fur being hydrophobic. "Uniquely structured to resist frost and moisture" claims more than anyone has demonstrated.

claims.claim: The wolverine's scientific name, Gulo gulo, literally means "glutton" in Latin.
claims.sourceCitation: Gulo gulo (wolverine). Animal Diversity Web, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology
claims.note: ADW: "The scientific name Gulo gulo comes from the latin word for glutton." Merriam-Webster traces Gulo to Latin for glutton or epicure, from gula, gullet. Worth knowing for tone: the "and the animal has absolutely earned it" follow-on is folklore. The gluttony reputation came via German Vielfrass, a folk etymology of an Old Norse name meaning roughly mountain cat, not from observed feeding behaviour.

claims.claim: Wolverines are opportunistic omnivores that will eat almost anything: carrion, small mammals, birds, eggs, berries, and roots.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine. Yellowstone National Park, National Park Service
claims.note: NPS Yellowstone: "Opportunistic eaters. Eat burrowing rodents, birds, eggs, beavers, squirrels, marmots, mice, and vegetation (including whitebark pine nuts)." Massé et al. 2023 (Front. Ecol. Evol. 11:1284901) describes wolverines as "facultative scavengers and generalist predators feeding on diverse prey ranging from small rodents to large ungulates." "Omnivore" is a slight stretch of the technical literature, which prefers generalist predator and facultative scavenger, but the diet list itself is fine.

claims.claim: They are famous for caching food, burying surplus meals in the snow or under rocks to retrieve later.
claims.sourceCitation: van der Veen, B., Mattisson, J., Zimmermann, B., Odden, J. & Persson, J. (2020). Refrigeration or anti-theft? Food-caching behavior of wolverines (Gulo gulo) in Scandinavia. Behavioral Ecology and Sociobiology 74:52. doi:10.1007/s00265-020-2823-4
claims.note: 303 caches identified from 38 GPS-collared wolverines. Wolverines "cache perishable food in snow, boulders, and bogs," year round, averaging 1.1 km from the food source. Inman et al. 2012 (J. Mammal. 93:634-644) frames this as the refrigeration-zone hypothesis: cold caching sites inhibit "insects, bacteria, and other scavengers."

claims.claim: Wolverines have semi-retractable claws, similar in concept to a cat's, which give them exceptional grip on ice and rock.
claims.sourceCitation: General Wolverine Characteristics. The Wolverine Foundation
claims.note: Contested, and the article states it as settled. ADF&G does say wolverines have "curved, semi-retractile claws," but The Wolverine Foundation, written by wolverine biologists, corrects this directly: "while biomechanics of the toes may suggest the claws are semi-retractile, anatomically they are clearly fixed." The cat comparison is the part that is clearly wrong. Nothing sources the "exceptional grip on ice" attribution to the claws specifically.

claims.claim: Despite their fierce reputation, wolverines are solitary animals. Adults come together only briefly to mate, and males play no role in raising young.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine. National Park Service species article (nps.gov/articles/wolverine.htm)
claims.note: The first half is right, the second half is the article's clearest factual error. NPS: "There is some evidence that males may play some role in brood-rearing, particularly after young reach 8 months of age." Copeland et al. 2017, "Social ethology of the wolverine" in Biology and Conservation of Musteloids (Macdonald, Newman & Harrington eds., Oxford University Press, pp. 389-398), proposes an ethological model revealing an intricate social organisation that "supports social behaviour that underpins offspring development," drawing on Glacier National Park telemetry showing adult males travelling with juvenile offspring. ADF&G also pushes back on the framing: "the 'bad tempered loner' stereotype gives the impression they are downright antisocial." (Note: I confirmed the Copeland chapter's existence and abstract wording through search results and the OUP catalogue listing, but the OUP chapter page itself is paywalled and I could not read the full text, so I have not included it in the sources block.)

claims.claim: A typical litter contains just two or three kits, born in late winter inside a snow den that the mother excavates herself.
claims.sourceCitation: Wolverine Species Profile. Alaska Department of Fish and Game
claims.note: ADF&G: "No litters larger than four have been reported in the wild and average 2-3 kits." The Wolverine Foundation puts mean litter size lower, at 1.8-2.0 (Magoun 1985, Copeland 1996, Persson et al. 2006), with births January to April and most in February to mid-March. On the den: NPS says "pregnant females build snow-dens" and "most dens that have been found consist of a complex of snow tunnels associated with boulders or rocks," so "excavates herself" is right but the dens usually incorporate boulders, downed logs or avalanche debris rather than being pure snow. Copeland et al. 2010 found all 562 known reproductive dens across Fennoscandia and North America sat on sites with persistent spring snow cover.

claims.claim: Wolverines live roughly 5 to 7 years in the wild, though individuals in captivity have reached 15 to 17 years, with the record standing at around 19.5 years.
claims.sourceCitation: AnAge: The Animal Ageing and Longevity Database, entry for Gulo gulo, Build 15 (record sourced to Weigl, R., 2005, Longevity of Mammals in Captivity)
claims.note: AnAge lists maximum longevity as 19.5 years in captivity, data quality "acceptable," sourced to Weigl 2005. ADF&G: "few wolverines live longer than 5 to 7 years in the wild. Some, however, do survive to 12 or 13 years." Animal Diversity Web gives up to 17 years in captivity. All three numbers in the sentence check out.

claims.claim: They were listed as threatened under the Endangered Species Act following a USFWS final rule in November 2023, reflecting habitat loss driven by climate change, which is reducing the deep snowpack they depend on for denning.
claims.sourceCitation: North American wolverine receives federal protection as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act. U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service news release, 29 November 2023
claims.note: Announced 29 Nov 2023, final rule published in the Federal Register 30 Nov 2023, effective 2 Jan 2024, covering the distinct population segment in the contiguous United States. USFWS: "Current and increasing impacts of climate change and associated habitat degradation and fragmentation are imperiling the North American wolverine." The snowpack-denning link is independently established by Copeland et al. 2010, which concluded that "reductions in spring snow cover associated with climatic warming will likely reduce the extent of wolverine habitat." Still listed as threatened as of 2026; critical habitat has not yet been designated.

corrections.claim: Wolverines have been documented displacing cougars from their kills. (Appears twice in the body, plus in the excerpt and meta description.)
corrections.problem: No primary source documents this. It traces to an uncited sentence on Animal Diversity Web that the popular web has copied endlessly. Camera studies of puma kill sites do not record wolverines, and the one peer-reviewed study of wolverine behaviour at shared carcasses (Bell et al. 2023) found wolverines avoiding a competitor at fine scale, not dominating one. ADF&G states outright that wolverines will not attack a larger predator. The article already contains the ADF&G bear correction in the same paragraph, so it contradicts itself.
corrections.suggestedFix: Cut the cougar claim entirely from both body paragraphs, the excerpt and the meta description. Replace with what is actually documented: wolverines are dominant scavengers at small and mid-sized carcasses and will bluff, posture and hold ground far out of proportion to their size, but no published study records one taking a kill from a cougar. In the pound-for-pound section, swap the cougar sentence for something like: "Wolverines will hold a carcass against animals far larger than themselves, and their willingness to escalate is genuinely unusual for a 30 pound animal. What the research does not show is a wolverine beating a cougar, wolf or bear off a kill. Biologists who study them say those stories are the most persistent myth about the species."

corrections.claim: Wolverines can smell prey buried under up to 20 feet of snow. That is not a typo.
corrections.problem: There is no primary source for 20 feet. The figure comes from an uncited PBS Nature web page tied to a 2010 documentary. Other popular sources give 6 feet or 2 metres, so the number is not even consistent. The "that is not a typo" line stakes the article's credibility on a number nobody has measured.
corrections.suggestedFix: Drop the specific figure and the "not a typo" aside. Rewrite as: "Wolverines find food by nose, and their range is remarkable. ADF&G biologist Howard Golden describes it simply: they can smell food over long distances or buried well under the snow. That is how they locate animals killed by avalanches or buried in winter snowpack, and they will dig through feet of compacted snow to reach a frozen carcass." That keeps the wow factor and loses the invented precision.

corrections.claim: Adults come together only briefly to mate, and males play no role in raising young.
corrections.problem: Directly contradicted by the National Park Service, which says there is evidence males play some role in brood-rearing, particularly after young reach 8 months. Copeland et al. 2017 in Biology and Conservation of Musteloids describes an intricate social organisation supporting offspring development, based partly on Glacier National Park telemetry showing adult males travelling with their juvenile offspring. ADF&G separately calls the antisocial-loner picture a stereotype.
corrections.suggestedFix: Rewrite the bullet: "Wolverines are usually solitary, but the bad-tempered-loner stereotype oversells it. Adults do come together to mate, and researchers now have evidence that males play a role once kits are older, roughly from eight months on. Telemetry work in Glacier National Park documented adult males travelling with their juvenile offspring, which upended the older assumption that fathers were absent."

corrections.claim: Wolverines have semi-retractable claws, similar in concept to a cat's.
corrections.problem: Contested, and stated as settled fact. ADF&G does use "semi-retractile," but The Wolverine Foundation, written by wolverine biologists, says that while the toe biomechanics may suggest semi-retractile claws, anatomically they are clearly fixed. The cat comparison is the weakest part.
corrections.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "Wolverine claws are large, strongly curved and built for digging and climbing. Some sources describe them as semi-retractile, though wolverine biologists note that anatomically the claws are fixed and the impression of retraction comes from how the toes move." Drop the cat analogy.

corrections.claim: They mark every inch of that range with a pungent musk secreted from glands near the base of the tail. This scent-marking system is so effective that other wolverines, predators, and even experienced trappers can detect it from a considerable distance.
corrections.problem: Wrong mechanism and a reversed chemistry claim. Wolverines have anal glands, a ventral gland near the belly and glands on the foot pads. The anal glands are used mainly as a fear-defence response, while routine chemical communication runs on urine and abdominal rubbing. And the only published chemical analysis of wolverine anal gland secretion found that the pungent thietanes and dithiolanes present in other mustelids are absent, meaning wolverine musk is less pungent than a skunk's or mink's, not more. The trapper detail is unsourced.
corrections.suggestedFix: Rewrite as: "They mark that range constantly, using urine and by rubbing a scent gland on their belly along rocks and logs. They also carry scent glands on the pads of their feet, so they leave a trail as they travel. The anal glands most people associate with the nickname skunk bear are mostly a defensive response rather than a marking tool. Chemists who analysed the secretion in 2005 found it lacks the sulphur compounds that make skunk and mink musk so overpowering."

corrections.claim: A home range of up to 240 square miles, one of the largest territories of any land mammal relative to body size.
corrections.problem: The 240 square mile figure is fine and even conservative, but the superlative is unsupported. Home ranges are documented as large relative to body size (Inman et al. 2012), yet no source ranks the wolverine against all land mammals on that metric.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: "A single male wolverine can patrol a home range of 250 square miles or more, and in the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem male ranges have averaged 350 square miles. Researchers describe those ranges as unusually large for an animal of this body size." That is stronger and it is actually documented.

corrections.claim: ...drag a full-grown caribou through deep snow...
corrections.problem: Wolverines do occasionally kill caribou and moose, but ADF&G describes such kills as rare, and NPS says they more often scavenge carcasses killed by other predators, drag them away from the kill site and cache them. No source documents a wolverine dragging an intact adult caribou.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: "...haul chunks of a moose or caribou carcass off through deep snow to cache them..." This keeps the image and matches what NPS actually describes.

claims.claim: The platypus was first described to European scientists in 1799 and was initially suspected of being a hoax; the describer cut into the specimen looking for stitches.
claims.sourceCitation: Discover Magazine, 'When Scientists Believed the Adorable Platypus Was a Hoax' (reputable science press; George Shaw, 1799, The Naturalist's Miscellany, described the animal as Platypus anatinus)
claims.note: Confirmed: 1799, George Shaw at the British Museum, name Platypus anatinus, and that he cut into the specimen checking for stitches. This is the one claim where I could only reach reputable science press; the Natural History Museum's own page (nhm.ac.uk/discover/the-platypus-puzzle.html) blocks automated fetching, so I did not cite it.

claims.claim: Monotremes are the only mammals that lay eggs, and there are exactly five living monotreme species: the platypus and four echidna species.
claims.sourceCitation: Zhou, Y., Shearwin-Whyatt, L., Li, J., et al. (2021). Platypus and echidna genomes reveal mammalian biology and evolution. Nature 592(7856):756-762. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-020-03039-0
claims.note: Paper states four echidna species (Tachyglossus aculeatus plus three Zaglossus spp.) alongside the single platypus species.

claims.claim: Out of roughly 5,500 mammal species on the planet, just five lay eggs.
claims.sourceCitation: ASM Mammal Diversity Database v2.5, American Society of Mammalogists Biodiversity Committee, released 28 July 2026
claims.note: The current authoritative count is 6,904 total mammal species, of which 6,791 are extant (6,774 living wild plus 17 domestic) and 113 recently extinct. 5,500 is closer to the Wilson and Reeder (2005) figure and is roughly 20% too low. The 'five out of thousands' point still stands, but the number needs updating to about 6,800.

claims.claim: A female platypus lays one to three leathery, soft-shelled eggs and incubates them by curling around them in a burrow for about ten days.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., Kingsford, R.T., Archer, M., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al.: 'one to three eggs ~12-15 mm diameter and ~15-17 mm long,' incubation '~10 days.' The Australian Museum gives 1-3 eggs (usually 2) and 'possibly 10 days.'

claims.claim: The platypus has no nipples; milk seeps through patches of skin on the mother's belly and the young lap it up.
claims.sourceCitation: Enjapoori, A.K., Grant, T.R., Nicol, S.C., Lefevre, C.M., Nicholas, K.R., Sharp, J.A. (2014). Monotreme lactation protein is highly expressed in monotreme milk and provides antimicrobial protection. Genome Biology and Evolution 6(10):2754-2773. DOI: 10.1093/gbe/evu209
claims.note: Paper states 'there are no nipples' and milk emerges from 'areolae... hidden by fur in platypus.'

claims.claim: The monotreme lineage branched off from other mammals over 166 million years ago.
claims.sourceCitation: Warren, W.C., Hillier, L.W., Marshall Graves, J.A., et al. (2008). Genome analysis of the platypus reveals unique signatures of evolution. Nature 453:175-183. DOI: 10.1038/nature06936
claims.note: Warren et al.: 'Estimates of the monotreme-theria divergence time range between 160 and 210 Myr ago; here we will use 166 Myr ago.' Worth noting the 2021 platypus/echidna genome paper (Zhou et al., Nature 592:756-762) revised this to about 187 Mya, roughly 21 Myr earlier, so 'over 166 million years' is safe but the modern figure is higher.

claims.claim: The bill contains around 40,000 electroreceptors and 60,000 mechanoreceptors.
claims.sourceCitation: Pettigrew, J.D. (1999). Electroreception in monotremes. Journal of Experimental Biology 202(10):1447-1454. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.202.10.1447
claims.note: Pettigrew 1999 states approximately 40,000 electroreceptors and approximately 60,000 mechanoreceptors, about 100,000 separately innervated receptors total. However the original counting study (Manger and Pettigrew 1996, Brain Behav Evol 48:27-54) reported 40,000 electroreceptors and 46,500 push-rod mechanoreceptors, and the San Diego Zoo fact sheet cites the 46,500 figure. Both numbers are in the published literature; 40,000 electroreceptors is solid, the mechanoreceptor count is 46,500-60,000 depending on source.

claims.claim: The platypus hunts underwater with its eyes, ears, and nostrils all closed, locating prey by electroreception.
claims.sourceCitation: Pettigrew, J.D. (1999). Electroreception in monotremes. Journal of Experimental Biology 202(10):1447-1454. DOI: 10.1242/jeb.202.10.1447
claims.note: Pettigrew: the platypus catches 'half its body mass of benthic invertebrates under water on the darkest night with all of its obvious sensory channels (eyes, ears and nostrils) tightly closed.' Corroborated by the Australian Museum species page.

claims.claim: Electroreception is the same basic principle used by sharks and rays but is extraordinarily rare among mammals.
claims.sourceCitation: Czech-Damal, N.U., Liebschner, A., Miersch, L., Klauer, G., Hanke, F.D., Marshall, C., Dehnhardt, G., Hanke, W. (2012). Electroreception in the Guiana dolphin (Sotalia guianensis). Proceedings of the Royal Society B 279(1729):663-668. DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2011.1127
claims.note: 'Passive electroreception is a widespread sense in fishes and amphibians, but in mammals this sensory ability has previously only been shown in monotremes.' The Guiana dolphin is the only known placental mammal with it, so the count of electroreceptive mammals is monotremes plus one dolphin.

claims.claim: Platypuses are born with teeth, lose them as juveniles, and replace them with hardened keratinous grinding pads; they store prey in cheek pouches to chew at the surface.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al.: teeth 'shed about a month after the young leave the nesting burrow'; 'A pair of cheek pouches lateral to the maxillary and mandibular keratinous grinding pads... store prey items collected underwater for mastication on return to the surface.' Note 'born with teeth' is loose, the vestigial teeth are shed in juveniles rather than at hatching, but the substance of the claim holds.

claims.claim: Male platypuses have a hollow spur on each hind leg connected to a venom gland in the thigh, and venom production peaks in the breeding season.
claims.sourceCitation: Whittington, C.M., Papenfuss, A.T., Locke, D.P., et al. (2010). Novel venom gene discovery in the platypus. Genome Biology 11(9):R95. DOI: 10.1186/gb-2010-11-9-r95
claims.note: Whittington et al.: glands 'increase in size during the spring breeding season.' San Diego Zoo fact sheet: spur about 1.5 cm, hollow keratin cone, adult males only, seasonal venom production.

claims.claim: Platypus venom will not kill a human but causes immediate, intense pain that can last for days or weeks and is resistant to standard painkillers like morphine.
claims.sourceCitation: Fenner, P.J., Williamson, J.A., Myers, D. (1992). Platypus envenomation, a painful learning experience. Medical Journal of Australia 157(11-12):829-832. DOI: 10.5694/j.1326-5377.1992.tb141302.x
claims.note: 1992 case: 'Pain was immediate, sustained, and devastating'; IV narcotics 'provided inadequate analgesia'; area 'remained painful, swollen and with little movement for three weeks' with impairment persisting three months. A regional nerve block was the effective treatment. Caveat: a 2025 MJA case (Moyer de Miguel et al., 222:387-389) had oxycodone reduce pain from 10/10 to 2/10, so opioid resistance is typical but not universal. No human fatality has been recorded.

claims.claim: The venom causes hyperalgesia, a heightened sensitivity to pain in the surrounding area.
claims.sourceCitation: de Plater, G.M., Milburn, P.J., Martin, R.L. (2001). Venom from the platypus, Ornithorhynchus anatinus, induces a calcium-dependent current in cultured dorsal root ganglion cells. Journal of Neurophysiology 85(3):1340-1345. DOI: 10.1152/jn.2001.85.3.1340
claims.note: Envenomation produces 'an immediate excruciating pain that develops into a very long-lasting hyperalgesia.' Corroborated by the 2025 MJA case report, where hot water immersion 'was not tolerated due to hyperalgesia.'

claims.claim: Researchers have found the venom contains over 80 different compounds, some of which are unique to the platypus and have no equivalent in any other venomous animal.
claims.sourceCitation: Whittington, C.M., Papenfuss, A.T., Locke, D.P., Mardis, E.R., Wilson, R.K., Abubucker, S., Mitreva, M., Wong, E.S.W., Hsu, A.L., Kuchel, P.W., Belov, K., Warren, W.C. (2010). Novel venom gene discovery in the platypus. Genome Biology 11(9):R95. DOI: 10.1186/gb-2010-11-9-r95
claims.note: Two errors. First, the 83 figure refers to predicted venom GENES/transcripts from a venom gland cDNA library, not confirmed compounds isolated from venom. Second, the paper's headline conclusion is the opposite of 'no equivalent in any other venomous animal': the 83 genes fall into 13 toxin families 'homologous to known toxins from a wide range of vertebrates (fish, reptiles, insectivores) and invertebrates (spiders, sea anemones, starfish),' which the authors present as evidence of convergent evolution.

claims.claim: Spurs are present in both males and females as juveniles, but females lose theirs as they grow up.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al.: 'juvenile females have vestigial spur sheaths, lost within the first year of life.' Whittington et al. 2010 adds that 'the venom system develops only in the male.'

claims.claim: The venom is thought to be used primarily in competition between males during mating season rather than for hunting or defence against predators.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Venom 'may have a primarily reproductive function, when males fight each other over access to breeding females.' Whittington et al. 2010 similarly: 'The venom system is thought to have a reproductive role.' Note both papers hedge ('thought to', 'may'), which the article's wording matches.

claims.claim: Venomous mammals form a short list including certain shrews and the slow loris.
claims.sourceCitation: Ligabue-Braun, R., Verli, H., Carlini, C.R. (2012). Venomous mammals: a review. Toxicon 59(7-8):680-695. DOI: 10.1016/j.toxicon.2012.02.012
claims.note: Venom occurs in Insectivora/Eulipotyphla (shrews, solenodons), Monotremata, Chiroptera (vampire bats), with Primates (slow and pygmy lorises) proposed. The article's list is correct but omits solenodons and vampire bats.

claims.claim: The webbing on the front feet extends beyond the toes for propulsion, and on land folds back so the platypus can walk and dig.
claims.sourceCitation: Australian Platypus Conservancy, 'Some platypus FAQs' (conservation organisation run by platypus researchers M. Serena and G. Williams, co-authors on Bino et al. 2019)
claims.note: APC confirms the first half directly: 'The platypus's front foot ends in a broad band of webbing that extends well beyond the end of its toes to assist swimming.' The fold-back-on-land detail is widely reported and almost certainly correct, but I could not confirm it in any primary or museum source I actually opened, the authoritative Fauna of Australia chapter (Grant, DCCEEW) timed out on fetch. Treat that half as unverified.

claims.claim: The tail acts as a rudder and serves as a fat storage organ.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: 'the tail is relatively sparsely furred and acts mainly as a fat storage organ, containing approximately 40% of the total body fat.' The San Diego Zoo fact sheet gives the same 40% figure (Temple-Smith 1973; Grant 2015). Australian Museum confirms the hind feet act as rudders.

claims.claim: The fur is dense and waterproof, trapping a layer of air next to the skin that provides insulation and buoyancy.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: 'The underfur retains air during dives, providing efficient insulation against heat loss.' San Diego Zoo: 'a layer of air trapped next to skin, body surface stays dry,' better insulation than polar bear or beaver fur. The insulation function is explicit in both; the buoyancy function is a physical consequence but was not stated in either source I read.

claims.claim: Platypuses typically stay underwater for 30 to 140 seconds per dive, though they can manage longer if needed.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al. give mean foraging dives of 30-140 s against an aerobic dive limit of 40-59 s; the Australian Museum gives the identical 30-140 s range. The 'longer if needed' is supported by the Australian Platypus Conservancy: about a minute aerobically, an extra minute and a half anaerobically, and up to 11 minutes when stationary and hiding.

claims.claim: The platypus is a carnivore feeding almost exclusively on small aquatic invertebrates: insect larvae (mayflies, caddisflies), worms, yabbies, shrimp and freshwater snails.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al.: predominantly 'aquatic macroinvertebrates from the orders Trichoptera, Ephemeroptera, and Odonata' (caddisflies, mayflies, dragonflies), plus chironomids and occasional freshwater crayfish. Australian Museum adds shrimps, swimming beetles, water bugs, tadpoles, worms, freshwater pea mussels and snails.

claims.claim: A platypus needs to eat roughly 20% of its body weight every day.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al. give 13-28% of body weight for non-breeding individuals, so 'roughly 20%' sits mid-range. The Australian Platypus Conservancy independently says 'as much as one-fifth of their body mass each day.' Worth adding: lactating females consume 90-100% of body weight daily, which is a far more striking number than the one the article uses.

claims.claim: It typically hunts at dawn and dusk; platypuses are most active at dawn and dusk.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: Bino et al. describe the platypus as 'predominantly nocturnal,' with 'some foraging occurs during daylight, particularly in winter or during lactation.' The Australian Museum says 'largely' active 'during twilight and in the night.' Crepuscular is part of the picture, not the whole of it. This matters because the article leans on 'most active at dawn and dusk' a second time as the rationale for the biofluorescence hypothesis, and the article's own closing paragraph calls them 'nocturnal,' contradicting itself.

claims.claim: The platypus has no stomach. Not a small stomach, not a simplified stomach. No stomach at all. Food travels from the esophagus directly into the intestine.
claims.sourceCitation: Dann, J., Qu, Z., Shearwin-Whyatt, L., van der Ploeg, R., Grutzner, F. (2024). Pseudogenization of NK3 homeobox 2 (Nkx3.2) in monotremes provides insight into unique gastric anatomy and physiology. Open Biology 14(7):240071. DOI: 10.1098/rsob.240071
claims.note: Directly contradicted. The paper states: 'The platypus stomach is small, amorphic, glandless and it lacks a pyloric sphincter, making it notably hard to distinguish from the oesophagus and intestines,' and describes monotremes as having 'truncated and aglandular antral stomachs.' What the platypus lacks is gastric glands, hydrochloric acid secretion, pepsinogens and (in the platypus specifically) a pylorus, not the organ itself. Bino et al. 2019 agree: 'Gastric glands and the genes involved in gastric function are absent.' The article's emphatic triple denial is the single biggest factual error in the piece.

claims.claim: The lack of a stomach is shared with a handful of other animals including lungfish and some species of carp.
claims.sourceCitation: Castro, L.F.C., Goncalves, O., Mazan, S., Tay, B.-H., Venkatesh, B., Wilson, J.M. (2014). Recurrent gene loss correlates with the evolution of stomach phenotypes in gnathostome history. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281(1775):20132669. DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2013.2669
claims.note: 'Holocephali (chimaeras), dipnoids (lungfish) and monotremes (egg-laying mammals) also lack acid secretion and a gastric cellular phenotype,' as do some teleosts (carp are agastric cyprinid teleosts). The article's list is correct but omits chimaeras.

claims.claim: The absence of a stomach is thought to be an ancient, ancestral condition rather than a recent adaptation, and the platypus may simply never have needed one.
claims.sourceCitation: Castro, L.F.C., Goncalves, O., Mazan, S., Tay, B.-H., Venkatesh, B., Wilson, J.M. (2014). Recurrent gene loss correlates with the evolution of stomach phenotypes in gnathostome history. Proceedings of the Royal Society B 281(1775):20132669. DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2013.2669
claims.note: Reversed. Castro et al. describe 'the stomach, a hallmark of gnathostome evolution' as an ancestral innovation, and stomach loss as repeated derived LOSSES: 'relaxation of purifying selection in pepsinogen genes and possibly proton pump genes in response to dietary changes led to the numerous independent events of stomach loss.' The genetic evidence is pseudogenised and deleted gastric genes, which only exist if the ancestor had a working stomach. So the platypus lineage did have one and lost it; it did not 'never need one.'

claims.claim: Researchers discovered in 2020 that platypus fur is biofluorescent, glowing blue-green under UV light, and the platypus was the first monotreme found to have this property.
claims.sourceCitation: Anich, P.S., Anthony, S., Carlson, M., Gunnelson, A., Kohler, A.M., Martin, J.G., Olson, E.R. (2021). Biofluorescence in the platypus (Ornithorhynchus anatinus). Mammalia 85(2):179-181. DOI: 10.1515/mammalia-2020-0027
claims.note: Published online 15 October 2020, print 2021. Fur appeared uniformly brown under visible light and green or cyan under UV, peaking around 500 nm; first report of biofluorescence in a monotreme. Important omission from the article: the study examined just THREE preserved museum study skins (Field Museum and University of Nebraska State Museum), not live animals. The De Gruyter full text is paywalled and blocks fetching, so the citation here is the Zenodo bibliographic record I opened; findings corroborated via Sci.News.

claims.claim: One leading hypothesis is that the glow plays a role in communication or camouflage in low-light conditions, since platypuses are most active at dawn and dusk when UV light is relatively more prominent.
claims.sourceCitation: Travouillon, K.J., Cooper, C., Bouzin, J.T., Umbrello, L.S., Lewis, S.W. (2023). All-a-glow: spectral characteristics confirm widespread fluorescence for mammals. Royal Society Open Science 10(10):230325. DOI: 10.1098/rsos.230325
claims.note: Later work substantially undercuts the adaptive framing. Travouillon et al. examined 146 specimens across 125 species, 79 families and all 27 living mammal orders, and found fluorescence in essentially all of them, concluding it is 'a ubiquitous property of unpigmented fur and skin' driven by tryptophan metabolite fluorophores masked by melanin in darker fur. They also compared preserved and frozen platypus specimens and found both preservation methods produced 'higher intensity fluorescence compared with the frozen specimen,' and specifically argued platypus ventral fluorescence is unlikely to be functional because platypuses 'hunt for aquatic prey underwater with their eyes closed.' The article's own 'possible byproduct with no function' alternative is now the better-supported reading.

claims.claim: Male platypuses have ten sex chromosomes (five X and five Y); females have ten X chromosomes.
claims.sourceCitation: Grutzner, F., Rens, W., Tsend-Ayush, E., El-Mogharbel, N., O'Brien, P.C.M., Jones, R.C., Ferguson-Smith, M.A., Marshall Graves, J.A. (2004). In the platypus a meiotic chain of ten sex chromosomes shares genes with the bird Z and mammal X chromosomes. Nature 432(7019):913-917. DOI: 10.1038/nature03021
claims.note: Confirmed by both Grutzner et al. 2004 and Warren et al. 2008 ('Males have five X and five Y chromosomes, which form a chain at meiosis and segregate into 5X and 5Y sperm').

claims.claim: The platypus sex-determination system is thought to be an intermediate step between the sex chromosome systems of reptiles and those of other mammals.
claims.sourceCitation: Grutzner, F., et al. (2004). In the platypus a meiotic chain of ten sex chromosomes shares genes with the bird Z and mammal X chromosomes. Nature 432(7019):913-917. DOI: 10.1038/nature03021
claims.note: The homology is specifically to the BIRD Z chromosome, not to reptiles generally: the largest X is homologous to the human X and another chromosome in the chain is homologous to the avian Z. Saying 'reptiles' is imprecise. Also, Zhou et al. 2021 (Nature 592:756-762) has since refined the story, showing the complex arose from an ancestral chromosome RING configuration via fusions and reciprocal translocations, which complicates the neat 'intermediate step' framing.

claims.claim: The platypus genome shares genes with mammals, reptiles, and birds, and sequencing it was a landmark moment.
claims.sourceCitation: Warren, W.C., Hillier, L.W., Marshall Graves, J.A., et al. (2008). Genome analysis of the platypus reveals unique signatures of evolution. Nature 453:175-183. DOI: 10.1038/nature06936
claims.note: The genome is described as 'a fascinating combination of reptilian and mammalian characters,' with chromosome organisation 'reminiscent of reptilian macro- and microchromosomes' and sex chromosomes sharing genes with the bird Z.

claims.claim: Platypus milk contains a unique antibacterial protein, and scientists are studying platypus milk proteins as a potential source of new antibiotics.
claims.sourceCitation: Enjapoori, A.K., Grant, T.R., Nicol, S.C., Lefevre, C.M., Nicholas, K.R., Sharp, J.A. (2014). Monotreme lactation protein is highly expressed in monotreme milk and provides antimicrobial protection. Genome Biology and Evolution 6(10):2754-2773. DOI: 10.1093/gbe/evu209
claims.note: Monotreme lactation protein (MLP) is 'present only in the monotreme lineage' and is 'an evolutionarily ancient component of milk-mediated innate immunity absent in other mammals.' Bino et al. 2019 corroborate. One caveat the article glosses: MLP is bacteriostatic against Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis only, with no effect on E. coli, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Staphylococcus epidermidis or Salmonella enterica. 'Might one day help us fight drug-resistant bacteria' is a fair hedge; anything stronger would not be.

claims.claim: The platypus is found in freshwater streams, rivers and lakes in eastern Australia and Tasmania.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058
claims.note: 'endemic to eastern mainland Australia, Tasmania, and adjacent King Island,' plus a small introduced population on Kangaroo Island, South Australia.

claims.claim: Numbers have declined significantly in recent decades and the species is now listed as Near Threatened on the IUCN Red List.
claims.sourceCitation: Bino, G., et al. (2019). The platypus: evolutionary history, biology, and an uncertain future. Journal of Mammalogy 100(2):308-327. DOI: 10.1093/jmammal/gyz058; and Australian Platypus Conservancy, 'Platypus conservation status'
claims.note: IUCN elevated the platypus to Near Threatened in 2016 (national listing in Australia upgraded 2014), on the basis that decline 'may potentially approach 30% of total population size over three platypus generations (estimated as a period of 21 years).' Also listed Vulnerable in Victoria and Endangered in South Australia. Note: iucnredlist.org blocks automated fetching, so this is verified via the peer-reviewed review plus the Australian Platypus Conservancy and the Australian Museum rather than the Red List page itself.

corrections.claim: Here's a fact that tends to stop people in their tracks: the platypus has no stomach. Not a small stomach, not a simplified stomach. No stomach at all. ... Food travels from the esophagus directly into the intestine, where digestion takes place.
corrections.problem: Flatly contradicted by the primary literature. Dann et al. 2024 (Open Biology 14:240071): 'The platypus stomach is small, amorphic, glandless and it lacks a pyloric sphincter, making it notably hard to distinguish from the oesophagus and intestines.' Monotremes have 'truncated and aglandular antral stomachs.' Bino et al. 2019 agree that what is missing is gastric glands and gastric-function genes, not the organ. The platypus lacks acid digestion and (uniquely) a pylorus; it does not lack a stomach.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'Here's a fact that tends to stop people in their tracks: the platypus has a stomach, but barely. It is small, shapeless, and completely glandless, and it has no pyloric sphincter to separate it from the intestine, so it is genuinely hard to tell where the esophagus ends and the gut begins. In most vertebrates the stomach is where food gets broken down by acid and enzymes. The platypus does none of that. It has lost the genes for stomach acid and for the digestive enzyme pepsin entirely, so food passes through that little sac essentially unchanged and digestion happens downstream in the intestine.'

corrections.claim: it's thought to be an ancient, ancestral condition rather than a recent adaptation. ... The platypus, which eats small prey continuously throughout its foraging sessions, may simply never have needed one.
corrections.problem: Backwards. Castro et al. 2014 (Proc R Soc B 281:20132669) describe the stomach as 'a hallmark of gnathostome evolution' and stomach loss as repeated, independent, derived losses: 'relaxation of purifying selection in pepsinogen genes and possibly proton pump genes in response to dietary changes led to the numerous independent events of stomach loss.' The evidence is pseudogenised and deleted gastric genes, which can only exist if the ancestor had a working stomach. The platypus lineage had one and lost it.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'It is not that the platypus never had one. The acid-secreting stomach is an ancient vertebrate invention, and the platypus lineage inherited it and then let it go. Researchers can still find the wreckage in the genome: the genes for stomach acid pumps and for pepsin are broken or missing outright. The leading explanation is that a shift in diet made those genes non-essential, so natural selection stopped maintaining them and they decayed. The same thing has happened independently in lungfish, chimaeras, and thousands of fish species. A platypus eating a steady trickle of soft invertebrates simply had nothing to lose.'

corrections.claim: Researchers have found that the venom contains over 80 different compounds, some of which are unique to the platypus and have no equivalent in any other venomous animal.
corrections.problem: Two errors in one sentence. Whittington et al. 2010 (Genome Biology 11:R95) identified 83 predicted venom GENES from a venom gland cDNA library, not 80-plus confirmed compounds isolated from venom. And the paper's actual headline finding is the opposite of the article's: the 83 genes fall into 13 toxin families 'homologous to known toxins from a wide range of vertebrates (fish, reptiles, insectivores) and invertebrates (spiders, sea anemones, starfish)' — presented as a striking case of convergent evolution, not uniqueness.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: 'When researchers sequenced the platypus venom gland, they turned up 83 candidate venom genes spanning 13 toxin families. The surprise was not that they were unique. It was the opposite: platypus toxins turned out to be built from the same protein families that show up in the venom of snakes, lizards, spiders, sea anemones, and starfish. Evolution appears to have reached for the same small toolkit again and again in animals that last shared an ancestor hundreds of millions of years ago.'

corrections.claim: Out of roughly 5,500 mammal species on the planet, just five lay eggs.
corrections.problem: Outdated by roughly 1,300 species. The ASM Mammal Diversity Database (v2.5, released 28 July 2026) lists 6,904 total mammal species, of which 6,791 are extant. 5,500 is closer to the 2005 Wilson and Reeder count.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'Out of roughly 6,800 living mammal species on the planet, just five lay eggs.'

corrections.claim: One leading hypothesis is that it may play a role in communication or camouflage in low-light conditions, since platypuses are most active at dawn and dusk when UV light is relatively more prominent.
corrections.problem: The adaptive framing has been substantially undercut since 2020. Travouillon et al. 2023 (R Soc Open Sci 10:230325) surveyed 146 specimens across 125 species, 79 families and all 27 living mammal orders and found fluorescence in essentially every one, concluding it is 'a ubiquitous property of unpigmented fur and skin' produced by tryptophan metabolite fluorophores that melanin masks in darker fur. They also found platypus fluorescence was MORE intense in preserved specimens than in a frozen one, and argued the platypus's ventral glow is unlikely to be functional precisely because platypuses hunt underwater with their eyes closed. The article should also note the original finding rests on three preserved museum study skins, not live animals.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace the paragraph with: 'Why does the platypus glow? The honest answer is that it probably is not special. The original 2020 finding came from just three preserved museum skins, and a 2023 survey of 125 mammal species spanning every living mammal order found fluorescence in essentially all of them. That team concluded the glow is a basic property of unpigmented fur and skin, produced by molecules that darker, melanin-rich fur simply masks. They also found that the preservation chemicals used on museum specimens can make the effect look stronger than it is, and pointed out that a glowing belly is unlikely to be signalling anything to a platypus that hunts underwater with its eyes shut. It is a real and genuinely lovely phenomenon. It just may not mean anything.'

corrections.claim: It typically hunts at dawn and dusk, making multiple dives in a single foraging session. / platypuses are most active at dawn and dusk
corrections.problem: Bino et al. 2019 describe the platypus as 'predominantly nocturnal,' with some daytime foraging particularly in winter or during lactation; the Australian Museum says 'largely' active 'during twilight and in the night.' Dawn and dusk is only part of the picture. The article also contradicts itself, calling them 'nocturnal' in the final section.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'It forages mainly at night, with activity spilling into dusk and dawn, making multiple dives in a single session.' And make the closing-section reference consistent.

corrections.claim: it's thought to be an intermediate step between the sex chromosome systems of reptiles and those of other mammals.
corrections.problem: Imprecise. Grutzner et al. 2004 report homology specifically to the BIRD Z chromosome (one chromosome in the chain), alongside homology between the largest X and the human X. Reptiles generally are not the comparison. Zhou et al. 2021 has since shown the complex derives from an ancestral chromosome ring formed by fusions and reciprocal translocations, which complicates the tidy 'intermediate step' story.
corrections.suggestedFix: Change to: 'This makes the platypus's sex-determination system one of the most complex in the animal kingdom. One of the chromosomes in the chain shares genes with the bird Z chromosome while the largest X shares genes with the human X, which is why the platypus has long been treated as a bridge between how birds and mammals sort out sex. More recent genome work suggests the arrangement began as an ancestral ring of chromosomes that fused and swapped pieces, so the picture is messier than a simple stepping stone.'
