claims.claim: The tusk is a modified left upper canine tooth that grows straight through the upper lip.
claims.sourceCitation: Nweeia MT, Eichmiller FC, Hauschka PV, Tyler E, Mead JG, Potter CW, Angnatsiak DP, Richard PR, Orr JR, Black SR. Vestigial tooth anatomy and tusk nomenclature for Monodon monoceros. The Anatomical Record 295(6):1006-1016 (2012). DOI 10.1002/ar.22449
claims.note: This paper specifically resolved the old incisor-versus-canine confusion: erupted tusks are surrounded by maxillary bone along the whole socket, so they are 'more accurately termed caniniform or canine teeth.' NOAA adds that the left tooth grows forward out through the front of the jaw.

claims.claim: The tusk sometimes reaches up to 10 feet (3 meters) in length.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) species profile. National Marine Fisheries Service.
claims.note: NOAA gives 'up to 9.8 feet long and weigh over 20 pounds.' Nweeia et al. 2009 give '2-3 m' as characteristic of adult males. 10 ft / 3 m is the top of the range, correctly framed as 'sometimes.'

claims.claim: Around 15% of females develop a tusk.
claims.sourceCitation: Garde E, Heide-Jørgensen MP. Tusk anomalies in narwhals (Monodon monoceros) from Greenland. Polar Research 41:8343 (2022). DOI 10.33265/polar.v41.8343
claims.note: Off by roughly a factor of ten. Direct sampling of 173 narwhals from Greenland hunts found tusked females at 1.5% of females, tuskless males at 2.8% of males, and double-tusked males at 0.9%. Louis et al. 2025 (Ecology and Evolution 15:e72376) use the same 1.5% figure and note Hay (1984) found similar frequencies in Canada. The 15% number traces to Roberge and Dunn (1990), a Canadian government technical report, and is repeated in Nweeia et al.'s 2009 Smithsonian chapter, but no direct-sample study supports it.

claims.claim: Occasionally a male narwhal will grow two tusks, though this is quite rare.
claims.sourceCitation: Garde E, Heide-Jørgensen MP. Tusk anomalies in narwhals (Monodon monoceros) from Greenland. Polar Research 41:8343 (2022). DOI 10.33265/polar.v41.8343
claims.note: Double-tusked males were 0.9% of males sampled. Nweeia et al. 2009 give 1.5% of narwhals overall, and note the second (right) tusk is slightly shorter with the same left-handed helix.

claims.claim: Virtually every narwhal tusk spirals in the same direction: counterclockwise, when viewed from the tip.
claims.sourceCitation: Kingsley MCS, Ramsay MA. The Spiral in the Tusk of the Narwhal. Arctic 41(3):236-238 (1988). DOI 10.14430/arctic1723
claims.note: The tusk is a left-handed helix, and when a right tusk also develops it twists left-handed too rather than mirroring the left. Kingsley and Ramsay note one historical exception, a dextral female tusk reported by Scoresby in 1823, so 'virtually every' is well chosen. NOAA independently describes it as 'spiraled to the left (counter-clockwise).' Minor pedantry: helix handedness is viewpoint-independent, so the 'when viewed from the tip' qualifier is unnecessary but not wrong.

claims.claim: The narwhal tusk is packed with up to 10 million nerve endings that connect to the outside world through tiny pores in the surface.
claims.sourceCitation: Biello D. Narwhal Found to Have a Trick Up Its Tusk. Scientific American, 14 December 2005
claims.note: The 10 million figure exists but describes tubules, not nerve endings. Scientific American reporting Nweeia's 2005 announcement says 'as many as 10 million tiny nerves reaching from its surface to the central core.' The published anatomy (Nweeia et al. 2009, Smithsonian at the Poles) describes a dentinal tubule network with lumena about 2 micrometres across, spaced 10 to 20 micrometres apart, running from the pulp through to orifices on the cementum surface. The nerves sit in the pulp; the tubules carry fluid movement to them. There is no published count of 10 million nerve endings.

claims.claim: The tusk is a hydrodynamic sensory organ: fluid movement within the dentinal tubules lets it register changes in water salinity, temperature and pressure.
claims.sourceCitation: Nweeia MT, Eichmiller FC, Hauschka PV, Donahue GA, Orr JR, Ferguson SH, Watt CA, Mead JG, Potter CW, Dietz R, Giuseppetti AA, Black SR, Trachtenberg AJ, Kuo WP. Sensory ability in the narwhal tooth organ system. The Anatomical Record 297(4):599-617 (2014). DOI 10.1002/ar.22886
claims.note: The mechanism is right (ocean water enters through cementum channels into patent dentinal tubules, signalling pulpal nerves via the maxillary division of the fifth cranial nerve, consistent with Brännström's hydrodynamic theory). But only salinity has been demonstrated in a live animal: the in vivo test showed 'significant changes in heart rate when alternating solutions of high-salt and fresh water are exposed to the external tusk surface.' Temperature and pressure detection remain hypothesised (Nweeia et al. 2009). The article presents all three as established.

claims.claim: Narwhals have been observed using their tusks to stun Arctic cod by slapping them with quick, precise strikes before eating them.
claims.sourceCitation: O'Corry-Crowe G, Ghazal M, Gillespie M, Galvin P, Harasimo J, Storrie L, Watt CA. Use of tusks by narwhals, Monodon monoceros, in foraging, exploratory, and play behavior. Frontiers in Marine Science 12:1518605 (2025). DOI 10.3389/fmars.2025.1518605
claims.note: Wrong fish. The only peer-reviewed documentation of narwhals striking prey with tusks is of Arctic char (Salvelinus alpinus), filmed by drone in Creswell Bay, Somerset Island, Nunavut on 4 and 6 August 2022, with hits 'of sufficient force to incapacitate, stun, and possibly kill the fish.' The Arctic cod version comes from a 2017 Fisheries and Oceans Canada drone-footage press release that was never published as a study.

claims.claim: Narwhals use their tusks in social sparring called 'tusking,' which is less about fighting and more about establishing social rank.
claims.sourceCitation: Graham ZA, Garde E, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Palaoro AV. The longer the better: evidence that narwhal tusks are sexually selected. Biology Letters 16(3):20190950 (2020). DOI 10.1098/rsbl.2019.0950
claims.note: Broadly right, but the peer-reviewed framing is male-male sexual competition rather than generic 'social rank.' The tusk shows hyperallometric growth and high variation, the signature of a sexually selected trait; the authors conclude it 'is a sexually selected signal that is used during male-male contests' and that 'tusking may be a ritualized behaviour used to assess the fighting ability of opponents.'

claims.claim: The narwhal tusk has no enamel coating, which means it is actually flexible, and it can bend up to 30 centimeters without breaking.
claims.sourceCitation: Brear K, Currey JD, Pond CM, Ramsay MA. The mechanical properties of the dentine and cement of the tusk of the narwhal Monodon monoceros compared with those of other mineralized tissues. Archives of Oral Biology 35(8):615-621 (1990). DOI 10.1016/0003-9969(90)90027-8
claims.note: Three separate problems. (1) The no-enamel part is correct: Nweeia et al. 2009 state 'the tubules in the narwhal tusk are not protected by an overlying layer of enamel.' (2) The causal link is wrong. Missing enamel is what makes the tusk sensory, not flexible. Flexibility comes from the tissue itself: Brear et al. found narwhal dentine 'considerably softer and less mineralized than human and cattle dentine,' with low Young's moduli, low yield stresses and high ultimate strains, closer to reindeer antler than to normal dentine. (3) The 30 cm figure is inverted. The source claim (Scientific American 2005, quoting Nweeia) is that an eight-foot tusk 'can yield at least a foot in any direction without breaking,' i.e. at least 30 cm, not up to 30 cm. The published measurements are flexural strength of 94.6 MPa at mid-tusk and 165 MPa near the base (Nweeia et al. 2009), with no bend-distance figure.

claims.claim: Narwhals live in Arctic waters of Canada, Greenland, Norway and Russia.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros): Unidentified Stock. Alaska Marine Mammal Stock Assessments (NOAA-TM-AFSC series)
claims.note: 'Narwhals are found year-round north of 60 degrees N, primarily in the waters of the Canadian Arctic, Hudson Bay, Baffin Bay, Davis Strait, West Greenland, East Greenland, and the waters around Svalbard, Franz Josef Land, and Novaya Zemyla.' Svalbard is Norway; Franz Josef Land and Novaya Zemlya are Russia.

claims.claim: Rather than avoiding the ice, narwhals actively seek it out, navigating narrow leads and cracks to find food and shelter from predators like orcas.
claims.sourceCitation: Breed GA, Matthews CJD, Marcoux M, Higdon JW, LeBlanc B, Petersen SD, Orr J, Reinhart NR, Ferguson SH. Sustained disruption of narwhal habitat use and behavior in the presence of Arctic killer whales. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114(10):2628-2633 (2017). DOI 10.1073/pnas.1611707114
claims.note: The ice-seeking half is fine: Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2015 found narwhals 'choose specific wintering grounds over deep water in the dense pack ice,' and Laidre et al. 2008 rate them the most specialised Arctic cetacean, overwintering in offshore ice-covered habitat. The orca-refuge half is not what the killer-whale study found. When killer whales were within about 100 km, 'narwhal were almost entirely constrained to a narrow band of water directly adjacent to shore,' i.e. they fled to shallow coastal water, not into ice. The paper reports no evidence of narwhals seeking ice when threatened.

claims.claim: They regularly plunge to depths of 1,500 meters (nearly a mile) and have been recorded going even deeper.
claims.sourceCitation: Hornby CA, Togunov RR, McClintock BT, Watt CA. Behavioural analysis of multi-year satellite telemetry data provides insight into narwhal (Monodon monoceros) winter prey selection in Baffin Bay. PLOS ONE 20(9):e0330928 (2025). DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0330928
claims.note: 'Regularly' is wrong. Weighted mean winter dive depth was 207 plus or minus 99 m, with maximum dives exceeding 1,400 m, and the authors describe dives 'possibly beyond 1500-1800 m (which we only see occasionally in the winter).' Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2015 recorded a January average daily maximum of 1,064 m (sd 323) with a single maximum of 1,600 m. NOAA gives 3,937 ft (1,200 m). So 1,500 m sits at the extreme end, not the routine end, and 1,600 m is the deepest figure I could find in a primary source.

claims.claim: In winter, narwhals make dives past 800 meters up to 25 times a day.
claims.sourceCitation: Laidre KL, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Dietz R, Hobbs RC, Jørgensen OA. Deep-diving by narwhals Monodon monoceros: differences in foraging behavior between wintering areas? Marine Ecology Progress Series 261:269-281 (2003). DOI 10.3354/meps261269
claims.note: Whales on one Baffin Bay wintering ground 'spent less time at shallow depths and most of their time diving to at least 800 m (13 to 26 dives per day, SE 1 to 3).' Note this describes one of two wintering grounds; whales on the other spent most time at 200 to 400 m.

claims.claim: Narwhals hunt Arctic cod, Greenland halibut and squid.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) species profile. National Marine Fisheries Service.
claims.note: NOAA lists Arctic cod, polar cod, turbot (Greenland halibut), squid and shrimp. Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2015 identify Greenland halibut as the likely target of deep winter dives.

claims.claim: Narwhals follow a seasonal migration into coastal fjords in summer and offshore deep water in winter, and these migrations are remarkably consistent from year to year.
claims.sourceCitation: Heide-Jørgensen MP, Nielsen NH, Hansen RG, Schmidt HC, Blackwell SB, Jørgensen OA. The predictable narwhal: satellite tracking shows behavioural similarities between isolated subpopulations. Journal of Zoology 297(1):54-65 (2015). DOI 10.1111/jzo.12257
claims.note: All 28 satellite-tagged whales showed the same migratory pattern, departing Scoresby Sound in September and reaching the continental shelf edge by November. The authors report 'remarkable similarity' in migration phenology, site fidelity, diving behaviour and habitat selection, and describe 'ocean-wide predictability in culturally inherited migration patterns.' One whale was recaptured less than 1 km from its tagging site 366 days later.

claims.claim: Narwhals lack a dorsal fin and have a low dorsal ridge instead, thought to be an adaptation for life under sea ice.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) species profile. National Marine Fisheries Service.
claims.note: NOAA confirms narwhals 'lack a dorsal fin' and refers to the dorsal ridge. The under-ice explanation is a long-standing hypothesis rather than a tested finding; the article's 'is thought to be' hedge is appropriate.

claims.claim: Narwhals travel in pods typically ranging from a few individuals to dozens.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) species profile. National Marine Fisheries Service.
claims.note: NOAA: pods 'generally consist of two to ten individuals, but may occur in large dispersed groups of hundreds to thousands.' The article's upper bound of 'dozens' is conservative rather than wrong.

claims.claim: Narwhals produce clicks, whistles and pulsed calls, using them both for echolocation and for communication.
claims.sourceCitation: Blackwell SB, Tervo OM, Conrad AS, Sinding MHS, Hansen RG, Ditlevsen S, Heide-Jørgensen MP. Spatial and temporal patterns of sound production in East Greenland narwhals. PLOS ONE 13(6):e0198295 (2018). DOI 10.1371/journal.pone.0198295
claims.note: Tag recordings separate three sound types serving two functions: echolocation clicks and buzzes for feeding, and calls (whistles and pulsed calls) 'generally thought to serve communication between conspecifics.' Buzzes clustered at 350 to 650 m during foraging; calls occurred mainly shallower than 100 m.

claims.claim: The word 'narwhal' comes from Old Norse nar ('corpse') plus hvalr ('whale'), because the mottled skin resembled a drowned sailor.
claims.sourceCitation: Harper D. narwhal. Online Etymology Dictionary
claims.note: This is the standard dictionary derivation but it is genuinely disputed, and the article states it flatly. Etymonline gives Old Norse nahvalr, 'corpse-whale,' from the 'whitish color, resembling that of dead bodies,' then notes the Germanic linguist Winfred P. Lehmann argued this is folk etymology and that nahvalr was a West Norse term meaning 'whale distinguished by a long, narrow projection,' i.e. named for the tusk. Also, the Old Norse element is nár, and the compound is náhvalr.

claims.claim: Young narwhals are born a uniform dark gray or brownish colour, lighten with age into a mottled pattern, and very old narwhals can appear almost entirely white.
claims.sourceCitation: NOAA Fisheries. Narwhal (Monodon monoceros) species profile. National Marine Fisheries Service.
claims.note: NOAA describes the sequence: young are 'uniformly brownish-gray,' juveniles develop 'white mottling,' and adults are 'white with black mottling on the head, flippers, dorsal ridge, and flukes.'

claims.claim: At their peak, narwhal tusks sold as 'alicorn' were worth ten times their weight in gold.
claims.sourceCitation: Mikolic A (Curatorial Assistant, Medieval Art). Hunting for a Unicorn Horn: Narwhal Tusks in Medieval Monsters. CMA Thinker, Cleveland Museum of Art, 6 September 2019
claims.note: The museum states a unicorn horn was 'worth ten times its weight in gold.' National Geographic phrases it more loosely as 'many times their weight in gold,' so this is a traditional figure rather than a documented market rate.

claims.claim: Queen Elizabeth I of England received a narwhal tusk valued at the equivalent of a castle.
claims.sourceCitation: Zimmer C. The Mystery of the Sea Unicorn. National Geographic, 18 March 2014
claims.note: The sources hedge this and disagree on the mechanism. National Geographic writes that Elizabeth 'was said to have paid 10,000 pounds for a unicorn horn, the price of a castle' (note 'was said to'), and separately that Martin Frobisher in 1577 'presented the horn to Queen Elizabeth, who commanded that it be kept with the crown jewels.' So one account has her paying and one has her receiving. This should be presented as a traditional account, not a fact.

claims.claim: Alicorn was believed to detect poison in food and drink, cure illness and protect the owner, and cups were carved from it for royalty.
claims.sourceCitation: Mikolic A. Hunting for a Unicorn Horn: Narwhal Tusks in Medieval Monsters. CMA Thinker, Cleveland Museum of Art, 6 September 2019
claims.note: The museum describes alicorn as in high demand for 'mystical medicinal properties' and specifically the poison test: 'if a horn was dipped in a liquid, it would bubble if poison was detected.'

claims.claim: It was not until the 1600s that European naturalists connected 'alicorn' to an actual animal, and the unicorn market slowly collapsed.
claims.sourceCitation: Mikolic A. Hunting for a Unicorn Horn: Narwhal Tusks in Medieval Monsters. CMA Thinker, Cleveland Museum of Art, 6 September 2019
claims.note: In 1638 the Danish naturalist Ole Worm concluded the traded horns were narwhal tusks and demonstrated it by displaying a complete skull with the tusk attached; afterwards 'trade in unicorn horns began to drop as well as its depiction in art.'

claims.claim: The Inuit knew what the tusks were, but the secret was kept by Norse and later Danish traders who controlled the supply.
claims.sourceCitation: Grimes K. Narwhal Ivory as the Arctic Colonial Speciality of the Kingdom of Denmark-Norway. Journal18: a journal of eighteenth-century art and culture, Issue 16 (Cold), Fall 2023
claims.note: The controlled-supply half is well documented: Grimes treats narwhal ivory as the territorial speciality of Denmark-Norway, held through dominion over Iceland and the Faroes, and the Danish Royal House says the same. The deliberate-secret framing traces to popular retellings (National Geographic writes that Vikings sold the tusks 'never revealing their origin'). I found no primary historical source establishing an organised, maintained secret, so I would soften rather than cite this.

claims.claim: The Throne Chair of Denmark, made in the 1600s, was constructed almost entirely from narwhal tusks and is on display at Rosenborg Castle in Copenhagen.
claims.sourceCitation: The Royal Danish Collection. The Knights' Hall (room 21), Rosenborg Castle
claims.note: Confirmed by three independent sources. The Royal Danish Collection places the chair in the Knights' Hall at Rosenborg, made 1662-1671 by Bendix Grodtschilling, used at coronations from 1671 to 1840. The Danish Royal House states 'the throne was produced of narwhal tusk, which the king had at his disposal by virtue of his dominion over the Faeroe Islands and Iceland.' Grimes (Journal18, 2023) describes it as 'constructed entirely from narwhal ivory with gold ornamentation.'

claims.claim: The Throne Chair of Denmark was believed to protect the king from evil and poison.
claims.sourceCitation: The Danish Monarchy (Kongehuset). The history behind the anointing throne
claims.note: None of the three official or academic sources on the chair says this. The Danish Royal House only notes 'it was said that the throne was made of unicorn horn, but in reality' it was narwhal tusk. Grimes (2023) explains its meaning in terms of divinely ordained royal authority: 'the soon-to-be king sat upon the throne, clutching the ivory arms, and only then received his divinely ordained authority as king.' The poison and evil claim looks like the general alicorn belief transplanted onto this specific object.

claims.claim: Narwhals and belugas are the only two living members of the family Monodontidae.
claims.sourceCitation: Skovrind M, Castruita JAS, Haile J, Treadaway EC, Gopalakrishnan S, Westbury MV, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Szpak P, Lorenzen ED. Hybridization between two high Arctic cetaceans confirmed by genomic analysis. Scientific Reports 9:7729 (2019). DOI 10.1038/s41598-019-44038-0
claims.note: 'Belugas ... and narwhals ... are the sole representatives of the Monodontidae family.'

claims.claim: At least one narwhal-beluga hybrid has been confirmed: a single skull recovered in West Greenland in 1990, DNA-verified as a narluga by Skovrind et al. in 2019.
claims.sourceCitation: Skovrind M, Castruita JAS, Haile J, Treadaway EC, Gopalakrishnan S, Westbury MV, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Szpak P, Lorenzen ED. Hybridization between two high Arctic cetaceans confirmed by genomic analysis. Scientific Reports 9:7729 (2019). DOI 10.1038/s41598-019-44038-0
claims.note: Accurate down to the detail. Skull MCE1356 was 'collected in 1990 from a hunter on an island in Disko Bay, West Greenland.' Genomic analysis identified it as 'a male, first-generation hybrid between a female narwhal and a male beluga,' and the paper states it 'would, to our knowledge, represent the sole evidence of hybridization' between the two species. Optional detail worth adding: the genome was about 54% beluga and 46% narwhal, and stable isotopes indicate it foraged differently from either parent species.

claims.claim: Narwhals can live close to 100 years, with some individuals reaching around 115, determined through aspartic acid racemization of the eye lens.
claims.sourceCitation: Garde E, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Hansen SH, Nachman G, Forchhammer MC. Age-Specific Growth and Remarkable Longevity in Narwhals (Monodon monoceros) from West Greenland as Estimated by Aspartic Acid Racemization. Journal of Mammalogy 88(1):49-58 (2007). DOI 10.1644/06-MAMM-A-056R.1
claims.note: The method is described correctly and the 115 figure is real, but it is one animal, not a norm. From 75 narwhals sampled in West Greenland, 'the maximum estimated age was a 115-year-old (plus or minus 10 SE) female.' That is a single extreme estimate with a wide error bar. NOAA's species page says narwhals 'live to at least 25 years old, and may live up to 50 years.' Garde et al. 2024 (Biology Letters 20:20240350) further show that age estimates for older narwhals carry real uncertainty: one whale aged 70 years by growth-layer counting came out at 55 by radiocarbon. Saying they 'can live close to 100 years' presents an outlier as typical.

claims.claim: Narwhals are considered one of the most vulnerable Arctic mammals to climate change.
claims.sourceCitation: Laidre KL, Stirling I, Lowry LF, Wiig Ø, Heide-Jørgensen MP, Ferguson SH. Quantifying the sensitivity of Arctic marine mammals to climate-induced habitat change. Ecological Applications 18(2 Suppl):S97-S125 (2008). DOI 10.1890/06-0546.1
claims.note: 'The hooded seal, the polar bear, and the narwhal appear to be the three most sensitive Arctic marine mammal species, primarily due to reliance on sea ice and specialized feeding.' The paper also calls the narwhal the most specialised Arctic cetacean and the most restricted in distribution.

claims.claim: As ice retreats, new predators like orcas gain access to waters that were previously frozen year-round.
claims.sourceCitation: Breed GA, Matthews CJD, Marcoux M, Higdon JW, LeBlanc B, Petersen SD, Orr J, Reinhart NR, Ferguson SH. Sustained disruption of narwhal habitat use and behavior in the presence of Arctic killer whales. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 114(10):2628-2633 (2017). DOI 10.1073/pnas.1611707114
claims.note: 'Given current reductions in sea ice and increases in Arctic killer whale sightings, killer whales have the potential to reshape Arctic marine mammal distributions and behavior.' The paper also found the disruption persisted for the full 10 days the killer whales remained in Admiralty Inlet, not just during attacks, which is a stronger detail than the article uses.

corrections.claim: Around 15% of females develop one, and when they do, it tends to be shorter and less pronounced.
corrections.problem: Off by about a factor of ten. Direct sampling of 173 narwhals from Greenland hunts (Garde and Heide-Jørgensen 2022) found tusked females at 1.5% of females, and Louis et al. 2025 repeat that figure, noting Hay (1984) found similar frequencies in Canada. The 15% number comes from Roberge and Dunn (1990), a government technical report, and is not supported by any direct-sample study.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "In almost all cases it is the males who grow the tusk. Only about 1.5% of females develop one, and when they do it tends to be shorter and narrower."

corrections.claim: Narwhals have been observed using their tusks to stun Arctic cod by slapping them with quick, precise strikes before eating them.
corrections.problem: Wrong species. The only peer-reviewed record of narwhals striking prey with their tusks is drone footage of Arctic char in Creswell Bay, Nunavut, in August 2022. The Arctic cod version comes from a 2017 Fisheries and Oceans Canada press release that never became a published study.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "In 2022, drone footage from Creswell Bay in Nunavut caught narwhals chasing Arctic char and hitting them with their tusks, striking hard enough to stun and possibly kill the fish. It was the first time anyone had documented the tusk being used to hunt."

corrections.claim: The narwhal tusk is packed with up to 10 million nerve endings that connect directly to the outside world through tiny pores in the surface.
corrections.problem: The 10 million figure describes dentinal tubules, not nerve endings. Nweeia et al. describe a tubule network with openings about 2 micrometres across, spaced 10 to 20 micrometres apart, running from the pulp out to the cementum surface. The nerves sit in the pulp and read fluid movement inside those tubules. No published source counts 10 million nerve endings.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "The narwhal tusk is riddled with as many as 10 million microscopic tubules that run from the pulp at its core all the way out to pores on the surface, putting the nerves inside the tooth in direct contact with seawater."

corrections.claim: The narwhal tusk has no enamel coating, which means it is actually flexible. It can bend up to 30 centimeters without breaking.
corrections.problem: Two errors. The missing enamel is what makes the tusk sensory, not flexible; the flexibility comes from narwhal dentine being softer and less mineralized than ordinary dentine, closer to reindeer antler (Brear et al. 1990). And the bend figure is inverted: the source claim is that an eight-foot tusk yields AT LEAST a foot (30 cm) in any direction without breaking, not up to 30 cm.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace the fun fact with: "The narwhal tusk has no enamel coating, which is why seawater can reach the nerves inside. It is also unusually bendy for a tooth. The dentine is softer and less mineralized than ordinary dentine, closer to reindeer antler, and an eight foot tusk can reportedly flex a foot in any direction without snapping."

corrections.claim: They regularly plunge to depths of 1,500 meters (nearly a mile) and have been recorded going even deeper.
corrections.problem: "Regularly" is wrong. Weighted mean winter dive depth is about 207 m, and dives past 1,500 m are described in the literature as occasional. The deepest single dive I found in a primary source is 1,600 m (Heide-Jørgensen et al. 2015). NOAA gives 1,200 m as the typical maximum.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "Most of their winter diving is far shallower than the headline numbers suggest, averaging around 200 meters. But they are capable of far more. Satellite tags have recorded dives past 1,400 meters, and one narwhal off East Greenland hit 1,600 meters, close to a mile down."

corrections.claim: Rather than avoiding the ice, narwhals actively seek it out, navigating through narrow leads and cracks to find food and shelter from predators like orcas.
corrections.problem: The ice-seeking part is right, but the orca-refuge part is not what the research shows. When killer whales were nearby, tracked narwhals crowded into a narrow band of shallow water directly against the shore, not into ice.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "Rather than avoiding the ice, narwhals seek it out, wintering over deep water in dense pack ice and using narrow leads and cracks to breathe and feed. When orcas do turn up, though, narwhals do not hide in the ice. Tracking data shows they flee into a thin strip of shallow water right against the shore, and stay pinned there for as long as the orcas remain in the area."

corrections.claim: They can live close to 100 years, with some individuals reaching around 115.
corrections.problem: Presents an outlier as typical. From 75 animals sampled, one female was estimated at 115 years plus or minus 10 by aspartic acid racemization. That is a single extreme estimate with a wide error bar. NOAA's species page gives at least 25 years and possibly up to 50, and a 2024 radiocarbon study showed age estimates for older narwhals can run high.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "They may be extraordinarily long lived. Scientists estimate narwhal age using aspartic acid racemization in the eye lens, and one female sampled in West Greenland came back at roughly 115 years, though with a wide margin of error. Most published estimates for the species are far lower, and how long a typical narwhal lives is still an open question."

corrections.claim: The word 'narwhal' comes from the Old Norse nar (meaning 'corpse') and hvalr (meaning 'whale').
corrections.problem: Stated as settled fact when it is disputed. The corpse-whale derivation is the standard dictionary one, but the Germanic linguist Winfred P. Lehmann argued it is folk etymology and that Old Norse nahvalr meant a whale distinguished by a long, narrow projection, i.e. named for the tusk. The Old Norse element is also nár, and the compound is náhvalr.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "The word 'narwhal' most likely comes from the Old Norse náhvalr, from nár ('corpse') and hvalr ('whale'). So the narwhal is, by the usual reading, the 'corpse whale.' Not everyone buys it: at least one Germanic linguist has argued the name originally described a whale with a long, narrow projection, and that 'corpse' is a later misreading. Still, the older explanation has a certain logic to it."

corrections.claim: The Throne Chair of Denmark ... was believed to protect the king from evil and poison.
corrections.problem: Not supported by any of the three official or academic sources on the chair. The Royal Danish Collection, the Danish Royal House, and the Journal18 study of Danish narwhal ivory all describe the material and the legend that it was unicorn horn, but none mentions a protective belief attached to the throne itself. Its documented meaning is divinely ordained royal authority.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "The Throne Chair of Denmark, built between 1662 and 1671, was constructed almost entirely from narwhal tusk, an Arctic commodity the Danish crown controlled through its dominion over Iceland and the Faroes. Legend held it was made from unicorn horn. Danish kings were anointed on it from 1671 to 1840, and it is still on display at Rosenborg Castle in Copenhagen."

corrections.claim: Queen Elizabeth I of England received a narwhal tusk valued at the equivalent of a castle.
corrections.problem: The sources hedge this and disagree with each other. National Geographic writes that she 'was said to have paid 10,000 pounds for a unicorn horn, the price of a castle,' and separately that Martin Frobisher presented her with a tusk in 1577. So one account has her buying it and one has her being given it, and both are traditional rather than documented.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "Queen Elizabeth I is said to have valued a unicorn horn at 10,000 pounds, roughly the price of a castle. In 1577 the explorer Martin Frobisher brought her a tusk taken from a dead narwhal on Baffin Island, and it was reportedly kept with the crown jewels."

corrections.claim: This makes it an extraordinarily sensitive sensory organ capable of detecting changes in water temperature, salinity, and pressure.
corrections.problem: Only salinity has been demonstrated in a live animal. Nweeia et al. 2014 measured significant heart rate changes when high-salt versus fresh water was applied to the tusk surface of live narwhals. Temperature and pressure detection remain hypothesized from the anatomy, not tested.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "This makes it a sensory organ. Researchers fitted live narwhals with a sleeve over the tusk and alternated salt and fresh water against it, and the whales' heart rates changed measurably. Salinity is the one stimulus confirmed so far. The same anatomy suggests the tusk could also register temperature and pressure, though that has not yet been tested on a live animal."

claims.claim: Tardigrades typically measure between 0.1 and 1.5 millimetres in length
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW gives 'average 0.1 to 0.5 mm'; Erdmann & Kaczmarek 2016 give 50-2,100 micrometres; Guinness World Records gives 1.5 mm for the largest species. The article's range sits inside the documented range.

claims.claim: They were first described by German zoologist Johann August Ephraim Goeze in 1773, who called them Kleiner Wasserbar, meaning 'little water bear'
claims.sourceCitation: The Public Domain Review, Among the Moss Piglets: The First Image of a Tardigrade (1773)
claims.note: Goeze's note appeared as pages appended to his German translation of Charles Bonnet's Traite d'insectologie. Erdmann & Kaczmarek 2016 independently date the discovery to 1773.

claims.claim: They have a plump barrel-shaped body with eight stubby legs, each tipped with tiny claws or suction discs
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW: 'four pairs of lobopodious legs terminating in adhesive pads, discs, or claws.'

claims.claim: Their mouth is a remarkable structure called a stylet, a hollow, needle-like tube they use to pierce plant cells or prey and suck out the contents
claims.sourceCitation: Guidetti R, Bonifacio A, Altiero T, Bertolani R & Rebecchi L (2015). Distribution of calcium and chitin in the tardigrade feeding apparatus in relation to its function and morphology. Integrative and Comparative Biology 55(2):241-252. doi:10.1093/icb/icv008
claims.note: The feeding apparatus has four parts: buccal ring, buccal tube, stylet system (two piercing stylets in stylet coats plus two supports), and the sucking pharynx lining. The stylets are solid, made 'exclusively of aragonite' (calcium carbonate), and are not the mouth. The hollow tube is the buccal tube, a separate structure. The article conflates the two.

claims.claim: There are around 1,500 described species of tardigrade
claims.sourceCitation: He Z-Y, Hu H-W, Lin Y, Zawierucha K, Nash M, Feng M, Yu D-T & He J-Z (2026). Flooded paddy soils exhibit higher tardigrade diversity than adjacent upland soils. Zoological Journal of the Linnean Society, zlag086. doi:10.1093/zoolinnean/zlag086
claims.note: States 'over 1500 tardigrade species have been identified', citing Degma & Guidetti's 2025 checklist. Note WoRMS still says 'about 1200 species'. Separately, the article's prose reads 'There are over around 1,500 described species' - a stray word that should be cleaned up.

claims.claim: You can find tardigrades in the Himalayas, in deep ocean trenches, in hot springs, in Antarctic ice, and in moss
claims.sourceCitation: Guinness World Records (2019). Tardigrades: are these the world's toughest animals?
claims.note: Hot springs, volcano interiors, Antarctic ice and moss are all documented (GWR; ADW: 'from the Arctic to the Antarctic, including great depths and altitudes'). 'Deep ocean trenches' is the weak link: published marine tardigrade collections top out around 4,700-5,400 m, which is abyssal, not hadal trench depth. Say 'the deep sea' rather than 'deep ocean trenches'.

claims.claim: The protective work in the tun state is done primarily by CAHS proteins, which form a gel-like matrix that physically stabilizes cell structures during desiccation
claims.sourceCitation: Yagi-Utsumi M, Aoki K, Watanabe H, et al. (2021). Desiccation-induced fibrous condensation of CAHS protein from an anhydrobiotic tardigrade. Scientific Reports 11:21328. doi:10.1038/s41598-021-00724-6
claims.note: CAHS1 oligomerises and 'formed a hydrogel', undergoing a sol-gel transition on drying. Boothby et al. 2017 independently show tardigrade disordered proteins vitrify (form amorphous solids) and are required for desiccation tolerance.

claims.claim: A sugar called trehalose is also present, but research by Boothby (2017) and Yagi-Utsumi (2021) has established it as a minor cosolute rather than the main protective agent
claims.sourceCitation: Nguyen K, KC S, Gonzalez T, Tapia H & Boothby TC (2022). Trehalose and tardigrade CAHS proteins work synergistically to promote desiccation tolerance. Communications Biology 5:1046. doi:10.1038/s42003-022-04015-2
claims.note: Two problems. First, mis-citation: Yagi-Utsumi 2021 does not test trehalose, it only notes CAHS function appears distinct from trehalose. Second, Boothby's own later work reverses the 'minor' framing: trehalose is present at only ~0.0019% but is a 'synergistic cosolute' whose presence is required for robust CAHS-mediated protection. CAHS proteins expressed alone 'provide little protection'. Trehalose is scarce, not unimportant.

claims.claim: A tardigrade in the tun state can remain in this suspended animation for decades
claims.sourceCitation: Roszkowska M, Goldyn B, Wojciechowska D, Ksiezkiewicz Z, Fialkowska E, Pluskota M, Kmita H & Kaczmarek L (2023). How long can tardigrades survive in the anhydrobiotic state? A search for tardigrade anhydrobiosis patterns. PLOS ONE 18(1):e0270386. doi:10.1371/journal.pone.0270386
claims.note: Under controlled laboratory desiccation, survival held above 80% to 120 days but collapsed to 1-6% at 240 days for two of four species tested. The authors explicitly note that anecdotal 20-plus-year reports 'were not conducted in strict laboratory conditions'. The decades-long records come from frozen (cryobiotic) storage, not dry tuns at room temperature. The two states should not be blurred.

claims.claim: Scientists have successfully revived tardigrades that had been frozen at -20 degrees C for 30 years
claims.sourceCitation: Tsujimoto M, Imura S & Kanda H (2016). Recovery and reproduction of an Antarctic tardigrade retrieved from a moss sample frozen for over 30 years. Cryobiology 72(1):78-81. doi:10.1016/j.cryobiol.2015.12.003
claims.note: Antarctic moss collected 1983, stored at -20 C for 30.5 years. Two adults and one egg of Acutuncus antarcticus recovered.

claims.claim: They simply added water, and the animals woke up, stretched their stubby legs, and went about their business as if nothing had happened
claims.sourceCitation: National Institute of Polar Research (2016). Animals revived after being in a frozen state for over 30 years. Press release accompanying Tsujimoto, Imura & Kanda, Cryobiology 72(1):78-81
claims.note: The paper's own framing is the opposite: 'The long recovery times of the revived tardigrades observed is suggestive of the requirement for repair of damage accrued over 30 years.' One of the two adults showed initial movement but died 20 days after rehydration. The survivor took about two weeks to crawl and feed, and its first egg took 19 days to hatch versus a 9.5-day median.

claims.claim: In 2007, the European Space Agency launched the FOTON-M3 mission
claims.sourceCitation: European Space Agency (2007). Lift-off for Foton microgravity mission. ESA press release, 14 September 2007
claims.note: Foton-M3 was a Russian-owned spacecraft launched on a Russian Soyuz-U from Baikonur Cosmodrome on 14 September 2007. ESA supplied the payload, including the Biopan-6 exposure facility that carried the tardigrades. ESA did not launch the mission.

claims.claim: Researchers exposed desiccated tardigrades to the full vacuum of open space, complete with cosmic radiation and ultraviolet radiation from the sun, for ten days
claims.sourceCitation: Jonsson KI (2019). Radiation tolerance in tardigrades: current knowledge and potential applications in medicine. Cancers 11(9):1333. doi:10.3390/cancers11091333
claims.note: Ten days in low Earth orbit, space vacuum at 10^-6 Pa, cosmic radiation 100 mGy, plus two UV spectra (UVA+B 280-400 nm at 7095 kJ/m2, and vacuum-UV to UVA 116.5-400 nm at 7577 kJ/m2).

claims.claim: Many survived vacuum exposure and cosmic radiation
claims.sourceCitation: Jonsson KI (2019). Radiation tolerance in tardigrades: current knowledge and potential applications in medicine. Cancers 11(9):1333. doi:10.3390/cancers11091333
claims.note: Samples shielded from solar light 'were not affected significantly by the exposure to cosmic radiation and space vacuum'.

claims.claim: Only three specimens of Milnesium tardigradum survived unfiltered solar radiation, and the survivors went on to reproduce normally after rehydration back on Earth
claims.sourceCitation: Jonsson KI (2019). Radiation tolerance in tardigrades: current knowledge and potential applications in medicine. Cancers 11(9):1333. doi:10.3390/cancers11091333
claims.note: The 'three specimens' figure comes from the initial short-term count in the 2008 letter. Jonsson's own later review states flatly that 'no animals of the two species survived the full UV spectrum'; the TARDIS project reported that the few UV-ALL animals that twitched back to life died within days. The animals that survived and reproduced were the 12% of M. tardigradum exposed to the narrower UVA+B spectrum, and the project reported their reproductive output was reduced relative to Earth controls. The article attaches the reproduction result to the wrong group and overstates 'normally'.

claims.claim: It was the first confirmed instance of any animal surviving direct exposure to the vacuum of open space
claims.sourceCitation: Jonsson KI (2019). Radiation tolerance in tardigrades: current knowledge and potential applications in medicine. Cancers 11(9):1333. doi:10.3390/cancers11091333
claims.note: Described as 'the first animals ever to survive the combined exposure of vacuum, cosmic radiation, and UV radiation under space conditions'. ScienceDaily's 2008 coverage of the paper frames it as the first time any animal had been tested under open-space conditions.

claims.claim: Humans begin suffering fatal radiation damage at around 4 to 5 gray (Gy)
claims.sourceCitation: Freeman ML (2025). Gastrointestinal acute radiation syndrome: current knowledge and perspectives. Cell Death Discovery 11:235. doi:10.1038/s41420-025-02525-6
claims.note: Human LD50 is 3.5-4 Gy without supportive care and 4.5-7 Gy with intensive medical intervention. The article's 4-5 Gy sits inside that band.

claims.claim: Tardigrades have a lethal dose (LD50) of roughly 5,000 Gy, about 1,000 times the human threshold
claims.sourceCitation: Horikawa DD, Sakashita T, Katagiri C, et al. (2006). Radiation tolerance in the tardigrade Milnesium tardigradum. International Journal of Radiation Biology 82(12):843-848. doi:10.1080/09553000600972956
claims.note: Median lethal dose at 48 h was 5000 Gy of gamma rays in hydrated animals (6200 Gy for heavy ions).

claims.claim: Hydrated, active tardigrades are marginally more radiation-tolerant than tuns, around 5,000 Gy versus 4,400 Gy, so it is not the tun state that drives this resistance
claims.sourceCitation: Horikawa DD, Sakashita T, Katagiri C, et al. (2006). Radiation tolerance in the tardigrade Milnesium tardigradum. International Journal of Radiation Biology 82(12):843-848. doi:10.1080/09553000600972956
claims.note: Exact figures: 5000 Gy gamma hydrated versus 4400 Gy gamma anhydrobiotic. Jonsson's 2019 review confirms the interpretation: 'The similar dose-response in desiccated and hydrated tardigrades seems to be a general feature, which is unexpected.'

claims.claim: Exposures above roughly 1,000 Gy can sterilize them even when they survive
claims.sourceCitation: Horikawa DD, Sakashita T, Katagiri C, et al. (2006). Radiation tolerance in the tardigrade Milnesium tardigradum. International Journal of Radiation Biology 82(12):843-848. doi:10.1080/09553000600972956
claims.note: Paper's stated conclusion: 'irradiation with >1000 Gy makes them sterile.'

claims.claim: In 2016 scientists discovered a tardigrade protein called Dsup (Damage Suppressor)
claims.sourceCitation: Hashimoto T, Horikawa DD, Saito Y, et al. (2016). Extremotolerant tardigrade genome and improved radiotolerance of human cultured cells by tardigrade-unique protein. Nature Communications 7:12808. doi:10.1038/ncomms12808
claims.note: Identified from the genome of Ramazzottius varieornatus.

claims.claim: This protein physically wraps around the tardigrade's DNA like a protective shield, preventing radiation from breaking the strands apart
claims.sourceCitation: Chavez C, Cruz-Becerra G, Fei J, Kassavetis GA & Kadonaga JT (2019). The tardigrade damage suppressor protein binds to nucleosomes and protects DNA from hydroxyl radicals. eLife 8:e47682. doi:10.7554/eLife.47682
claims.note: Dsup does not wrap around DNA. It is a nucleosome-binding protein that preferentially binds nucleosomal chromatin over free DNA and shields it from hydroxyl radicals; a conserved region resembles the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins. Hashimoto 2016 describes it forming large DNA-Dsup complexes, not a wrapping. In a nucleosome it is DNA that wraps around protein, so the image is backwards.

claims.claim: Researchers transferred the Dsup gene into human cells, where it reduced radiation-induced DNA damage by around 40%
claims.sourceCitation: Hashimoto T, Horikawa DD, Saito Y, et al. (2016). Extremotolerant tardigrade genome and improved radiotolerance of human cultured cells by tardigrade-unique protein. Nature Communications 7:12808. doi:10.1038/ncomms12808
claims.note: Approximately 40% reduction in gamma-H2AX foci; comet assay showed tail DNA fall from 33% to 16% after 10 Gy.

claims.claim: Tardigrades can survive temperatures as low as -272 degrees C, just one degree above absolute zero
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW gives survival 'at temperatures ranging from 149 C to -272 C'. Erdmann & Kaczmarek 2016 trace the figure to Becquerel (1950), who revived animals after cooling to -272.8 C, and to earlier liquid-helium immersion work by Rahm. This is an anhydrobiotic-state result, worth noting.

claims.claim: Neves et al. (2020, Scientific Reports) found active tardigrades have a median lethal temperature of 37.1 degrees C; tuns die at 82.7 degrees C for one hour or 63.1 degrees C for 24 hours
claims.sourceCitation: Neves RC, Hvidepil LKB, Sorensen-Hygum TL, Stuart RM & Mobjerg N (2020). Thermotolerance experiments on active and desiccated states of Ramazzottius varieornatus emphasize that tardigrades are sensitive to high temperatures. Scientific Reports 10:94. doi:10.1038/s41598-019-56965-z
claims.note: Exact match on all three figures. Non-acclimated active 24h LT50 37.1 C (acclimated 37.6 C); tuns 82.7 C at 1 h and 63.1 C at 24 h. Species is Ramazzottius varieornatus, worth naming since the article generalises to all tardigrades.

claims.claim: Tardigrades have been subjected to pressures six times greater than those found at the bottom of the Mariana Trench, and survived
claims.sourceCitation: Horikawa DD, Kawai K, Koseki S, Iwata K, Okuda T & Yamamoto K (2007). High hydrostatic pressure tolerance of tardigrades. High Pressure Bioscience and Biotechnology 1(1):157-160. doi:10.11229/hpbb.1.157
claims.note: Conservative, if anything. Anhydrobiotic tardigrades had already been shown to tolerate 0.6 GPa (Seki & Toyoshima 1998, Nature 395:853-854), roughly 5.5x the ~110 MPa at the Challenger Deep. Horikawa's own work took anhydrobiotic Milnesium tardigradum to 1.2 GPa with all individuals active 24 h later, while no hydrated animals moved. Guinness World Records also states 'six times higher than those at the deepest parts of the ocean'.

claims.claim: Scientists in Japan revived tardigrades in 2016 that had been frozen since 1983, and the animals went on to reproduce normally
claims.sourceCitation: National Institute of Polar Research (2016). Animals revived after being in a frozen state for over 30 years; and Tsujimoto M, Imura S & Kanda H (2016). Cryobiology 72(1):78-81
claims.note: Two errors. The revival was in May 2014; 2016 is the publication year. And reproduction was not normal: the surviving adult took about two weeks to crawl and feed, laid 19 eggs of which 14 hatched, and its first egg needed 19 days versus a 9.5-day median. Only the hatchling from the revived egg developed without apparent defects.

claims.claim: Tardigrades almost certainly survived all five mass extinctions, but the fossil record offers only indirect support; only a handful of body fossils are known and the oldest unambiguously modern-looking specimens date to the Cretaceous
claims.sourceCitation: Mapalo MA, Wolfe JM & Ortega-Hernandez J (2024). Cretaceous amber inclusions illuminate the evolutionary origin of tardigrades. Communications Biology 7:953. doi:10.1038/s42003-024-06643-2
claims.note: Accurate and unusually well hedged. Four confirmed crown-group tardigrade body fossils exist, all in amber; the oldest is Milnesium swolenskyi from Turonian New Jersey amber (89.8-93.9 Ma). The Cambrian Orsten specimen 'lacks characters defining extant tardigrades, and therefore can only be regarded as part of the stem group'.

claims.claim: They have been on Earth for at least 530 million years
claims.sourceCitation: Mapalo MA, Wolfe JM & Ortega-Hernandez J (2024). Cretaceous amber inclusions illuminate the evolutionary origin of tardigrades. Communications Biology 7:953. doi:10.1038/s42003-024-06643-2
claims.note: The current best molecular estimate for crown-group Tardigrada is a mean of about 499 Ma with a 95% HPD spanning 613.66-380.5 Ma. Older studies gave Precambrian dates of 627-691 Ma. A flat 'at least 530 million years' presents a wide, contested confidence interval as a hard floor, and 530 Ma is not any published point estimate.

claims.claim: The only scenarios that might finally do them in are the sun expanding into a red giant, or a nearby gamma-ray burst powerful enough to strip away Earth's atmosphere entirely
claims.sourceCitation: Sloan D, Alves Batista R & Loeb A (2017). The Resilience of Life to Astrophysical Events. Scientific Reports 7:5419. doi:10.1038/s41598-017-05796-x
claims.note: The mechanism is wrong. Sloan et al. define total sterilisation as boiling the oceans, not stripping the atmosphere. And they do not treat a gamma-ray burst as a live threat: a GRB would have to occur within about 40 light years, at an estimated probability of ~3.2 x 10^-10 per billion years, and supernovae would need to be within 0.04 parsecs. Their finding is that all three astrophysical sources are effectively negligible, leaving stellar evolution as the endpoint.

claims.claim: In April 2019 the Israeli spacecraft Beresheet crashed into the moon's Sea of Serenity, carrying dehydrated tardigrades sent by the Arch Mission Foundation
claims.sourceCitation: NASA (2019). LRO Spots Beresheet Impact Site. NASA Goddard, 15 May 2019
claims.note: NASA confirms the 11 April 2019 hard landing in Mare Serenitatis and the ~10 m dark impact smudge imaged by LRO on 22 April. EarthSky documents the Arch Mission Foundation Lunar Library and 'a few thousand' dehydrated tardigrades. One quibble: 'scattering its payload' overstates it, since the foundation reported the nickel library likely stayed largely intact, and NASA notes the low-angle (8.4 degree), relatively low-velocity impact left no deep crater.

claims.claim: Traspas and Burchell (2021, Astrobiology) established that tardigrade tuns do not survive impacts above roughly 900 m/s or pressures above 1.14 gigapascals
claims.sourceCitation: Traspas A & Burchell MJ (2021). Tardigrade Survival Limits in High-Speed Impacts: Implications for Panspermia and Collection of Samples from Plumes Emitted by Ice Worlds. Astrobiology 21(7):845-852. doi:10.1089/ast.2020.2405
claims.note: Exact: survival at 0.728 km/s (0.86 GPa), none at 0.901 km/s (1.14 GPa). Method was frozen Hypsibius dujardini in water-filled nylon projectiles fired into sand.

claims.claim: Beresheet's impact exceeded both thresholds. The tardigrades almost certainly did not survive.
claims.sourceCitation: Palka L (2024). Could tardigrades have colonized the Moon? The Conversation, 26 February 2024 (author: Maitre de conferences, Museum national d'histoire naturelle, Paris)
claims.note: This is an inference, not a finding of the cited paper: Traspas & Burchell never mention Beresheet, the Moon, or the Arch Mission. On the numbers it is genuinely marginal. Palka gives Beresheet at about 3,000 km/h (~833 m/s) at 150 m altitude, which is below the 901 m/s lethal threshold, and concludes the tardigrades 'might have endured the impact itself'. The defensible argument is the one Burchell made in press interviews, that a metal spacecraft frame striking rock generates shock pressure far above 1.14 GPa. The article should either attribute that reasoning correctly or soften to 'probably did not survive'.

claims.claim: The idea that tardigrades could colonize the moon is wrong
claims.sourceCitation: Palka L (2024). Could tardigrades have colonized the Moon? The Conversation, 26 February 2024
claims.note: Correct conclusion, but the article reaches it via impact physics when the decisive reason is simpler and stronger: reviving and reproducing requires liquid water, oxygen and food, none of which exist on the Moon, so 'their colonising the Moon is thus impossible' regardless of whether any survived the crash.

claims.claim: Tardigrades have a brain and a nervous system, with a distinct head, sensory organs and a central nervous system
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW describes 'a large, dorsal, lobed cerebral ganglion connected to a subesophageal ganglion', plus paired ventral nerve cords and a chain of four leg ganglia.

claims.claim: Certain tardigrade species eat other tardigrades, making them cannibalistic predators
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Milnesium tardigradum, University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: M. tardigradum is 'an omnivorous predator that actively hunts its prey' and has been recorded feeding on smaller tardigrades in the genera Diphascon and Hypsibius. Strictly this is interspecific predation rather than cannibalism in the narrow sense, though the term is used loosely in the literature.

claims.claim: Many species reproduce sexually while others reproduce asexually through parthenogenesis, and some do both
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: Many terrestrial species are parthenogenetic or self-fertilising hermaphrodites; aquatic species are typically dioecious. The Milnesium account confirms both modes in one species.

claims.claim: Females of some species shed their cuticle and lay eggs directly inside it, using the molted skin as a protective egg case
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW: some species deposit eggs 'in the female's shed cuticle'.

claims.claim: Under normal conditions most species live for only a few months to a few years
claims.sourceCitation: Animal Diversity Web, Tardigrada (water bears), University of Michigan Museum of Zoology (accessed 2026)
claims.note: ADW: outside cryptobiosis they 'generally live 3 to 30 months'. The Milnesium account gives captive lifespans of under 14 to 58 days, averaging 40. 'A few months to about two years' would be tighter than 'a few years'.

claims.claim: It has conquered every environment on the planet, survived every catastrophe in Earth's history, traveled to space, and may currently be sitting on the surface of the moon
claims.sourceCitation: Mapalo MA, Wolfe JM & Ortega-Hernandez J (2024). Cretaceous amber inclusions illuminate the evolutionary origin of tardigrades. Communications Biology 7:953. doi:10.1038/s42003-024-06643-2
claims.note: The closing paragraph reverts to the flat claim the article had carefully hedged two sections earlier. With four amber body fossils, none older than the Turonian, there is no fossil documentation of tardigrades through any mass extinction. The conclusion should match the body of the article.

corrections.claim: A sugar called trehalose is also present, but research by Boothby (2017) and Yagi-Utsumi (2021) has established it as a minor cosolute rather than the main protective agent.
corrections.problem: Mis-cited and superseded. Yagi-Utsumi 2021 does not test trehalose at all. And Boothby's own 2022 follow-up shows trehalose, though present at only ~0.0019%, is a synergistic cosolute that is required for robust CAHS protection: CAHS proteins expressed alone 'provide little protection'. Scarce is not the same as minor.
corrections.suggestedFix: A sugar called trehalose is also present, but tardigrades carry only trace amounts of it, far less than other drying-tolerant animals. Rather than being the main protective agent on its own, it appears to work synergistically with the CAHS proteins, which provide little protection without it (Nguyen et al., 2022).

corrections.claim: A tardigrade in the tun state can remain in this suspended animation for decades
corrections.problem: Conflates dry anhydrobiosis with frozen storage. Under controlled laboratory desiccation, survival held above 80% to 120 days but collapsed to 1-6% at 240 days in two of four species tested. The decades-long records all come from animals frozen at -20 C, not dry tuns.
corrections.suggestedFix: A tardigrade in the tun state can hold out for months, though controlled experiments show dry survival dropping off sharply within a year. The record-breaking cases involve freezing rather than simple drying: scientists have revived tardigrades that spent 30 years at -20 degrees C.

corrections.claim: They simply added water, and the animals woke up, stretched their stubby legs, and went about their business as if nothing had happened.
corrections.problem: Directly contradicted by the paper. One of the two revived adults died 20 days after rehydration. The survivor took about two weeks to crawl and feed, and its first egg needed 19 days to hatch against a 9.5-day median. The authors read the long recovery as evidence of damage repair.
corrections.suggestedFix: They added water, and the animals came back. Recovery was slow and imperfect: one of the two adults died within three weeks, and the survivor took a fortnight before it could crawl and feed. Its first egg took twice as long as normal to hatch, which the researchers read as the cost of 30 years of accumulated damage.

corrections.claim: In 2007, the European Space Agency launched the FOTON-M3 mission
corrections.problem: Foton-M3 was a Russian spacecraft launched on a Russian Soyuz-U from Baikonur Cosmodrome on 14 September 2007. ESA's role was supplying the payload, including the Biopan-6 exposure facility that carried the tardigrades.
corrections.suggestedFix: In 2007, the Russian Foton-M3 spacecraft lifted off from Baikonur carrying a European Space Agency payload called Biopan-6, and tucked inside were some very unusual passengers: tardigrades.

corrections.claim: Full solar UV proved far more lethal: only three specimens of Milnesium tardigradum survived unfiltered solar radiation. The survivors went on to reproduce normally after rehydration back on Earth.
corrections.problem: Two problems. The three UV-ALL specimens revived but did not persist, and Jönsson's own 2019 review states plainly that no animals of either species survived the full UV spectrum. Separately, the animals that survived and reproduced were the 12% of M. tardigradum exposed to the narrower UVA+B band, and their reproductive output was reduced relative to Earth controls.
corrections.suggestedFix: Full solar UV proved far more lethal. A handful of Milnesium tardigradum briefly stirred after exposure to the unfiltered spectrum, but none ultimately survived it. Under the narrower UVA and UVB band, 12% came through, and those survivors did reproduce after rehydration back on Earth, though with reduced output compared to ground controls.

corrections.claim: This protein physically wraps around the tardigrade's DNA like a protective shield, preventing radiation from breaking the strands apart.
corrections.problem: Wrong mechanism, and the image is backwards. Dsup is a nucleosome-binding protein that preferentially binds chromatin over naked DNA and shields it from hydroxyl radicals; part of it resembles the nucleosome-binding domain of vertebrate HMGN proteins. In a nucleosome, DNA wraps around protein, not the reverse.
corrections.suggestedFix: This protein binds to nucleosomes, the spools of protein that chromosomal DNA is wound around, and shields that packaged DNA from the hydroxyl radicals radiation generates. It prevents damage rather than repairing it after the fact.

corrections.claim: Scientists in Japan revived tardigrades in 2016 that had been frozen since 1983, and the animals went on to reproduce normally.
corrections.problem: The revival happened in May 2014; 2016 is the publication year. And reproduction was not normal: delayed hatching, reduced viability, and one of the two adults died 20 days in.
corrections.suggestedFix: Scientists in Japan thawed a moss sample in 2014 that had been frozen since 1983, and published the results in 2016. Two adults and one egg revived. One adult died within three weeks; the other reproduced, though its eggs took roughly twice as long as normal to hatch.

corrections.claim: They have been on Earth for at least 530 million years, predating the dinosaurs by hundreds of millions of years.
corrections.problem: 530 Ma is not a published point estimate and is presented as a hard floor. The current best molecular estimate for crown-group Tardigrada is a mean of about 499 Ma with a 95% credible interval spanning 614 to 380 Ma; older studies put it as far back as 627 to 691 Ma.
corrections.suggestedFix: Molecular clock estimates place the origin of modern tardigrades somewhere around the middle Cambrian, roughly 500 million years ago, though the uncertainty on that figure is wide. Either way, they predate the dinosaurs by hundreds of millions of years.

corrections.claim: The only scenarios that might finally do them in are truly cosmic in scale: the eventual expansion of the sun into a red giant, or a nearby gamma-ray burst powerful enough to strip away Earth's atmosphere entirely.
corrections.problem: The sterilisation criterion in the cited study is boiling the oceans, not stripping the atmosphere. And the study's actual finding is that gamma-ray bursts are effectively not a threat: one would have to occur within roughly 40 light years, at a probability of about 3 in 10 billion per billion years.
corrections.suggestedFix: Physicists have run the numbers on what it would take to sterilise the planet by boiling away its oceans. Asteroid impacts, supernovae and gamma-ray bursts all turn out to be far too weak or far too rare to manage it. That leaves the sun itself: when it eventually expands and the oceans boil off, the tardigrades go too.

corrections.claim: Research by Traspas and Burchell (2021, Astrobiology) established that tardigrade tuns do not survive impacts above roughly 900 m/s or pressures above 1.14 gigapascals. Beresheet's impact exceeded both thresholds. The tardigrades almost certainly did not survive.
corrections.problem: The cited paper never mentions Beresheet, the Moon, or the Arch Mission, so the conclusion is an inference presented as a finding. On the raw numbers it is marginal: Beresheet was reported at roughly 3,000 km/h (about 833 m/s) at 150 m altitude, just under the 901 m/s threshold, and one academic assessment concludes the tardigrades 'might have endured the impact itself'. The stronger version of the argument is about shock pressure from a metal spacecraft frame hitting rock, not impact speed.
corrections.suggestedFix: Impact experiments by Traspas and Burchell (2021) found that tardigrade tuns survive impacts up to about 730 m/s but not at 900 m/s, which corresponds to shock pressures above 1.14 gigapascals. Beresheet hit at roughly that speed, and the shock from a metal lander striking rock would have been considerably higher than anything the tuns endured in the lab. The tardigrades probably did not survive. What is certain is that they can never revive there: rehydration needs liquid water, and the Moon has none.

corrections.claim: Their mouth is a remarkable structure called a stylet, a hollow, needle-like tube they use to pierce plant cells or prey and suck out the contents.
corrections.problem: Conflates two separate structures. Tardigrades have a pair of piercing stylets composed almost entirely of aragonite (calcium carbonate), which are solid, and a separate hollow buccal tube leading to a muscular sucking pharynx. The stylets are not the mouth.
corrections.suggestedFix: Their feeding apparatus is a remarkable piece of engineering: a pair of solid piercing stylets made of calcium carbonate that puncture plant cells or prey, and a hollow buccal tube behind them connected to a muscular sucking pharynx that draws out the contents.

corrections.claim: it has conquered every environment on the planet, survived every catastrophe in Earth's history, traveled to space, and may currently be sitting on the surface of the moon
corrections.problem: The closing paragraph reasserts the flat claim the article had carefully qualified two sections earlier. With only four crown-group body fossils, none older than about 90 million years, there is no fossil documentation of tardigrades through any mass extinction.
corrections.suggestedFix: it has colonised nearly every habitat on the planet, almost certainly rode out every mass extinction, travelled to space, and may currently be sitting on the surface of the moon

corrections.claim: You can find tardigrades in the Himalayas, in deep ocean trenches, in hot springs, in Antarctic ice, and in the moss growing on the wall outside your window.
corrections.problem: Hot springs, Antarctic ice, high altitude and moss are all documented, but published marine tardigrade collections reach roughly 4,700 to 5,400 m, which is abyssal seafloor rather than hadal trench depth.
corrections.suggestedFix: You can find tardigrades in the Himalayas, on the deep-sea floor thousands of metres down, in hot springs, in Antarctic ice, and in the moss growing on the wall outside your window.

claims.claim: The axolotl is pronounced "ax-uh-lot-ul"
claims.sourceCitation: Merriam-Webster. "Axolotl." Merriam-Webster.com Dictionary (accessed 2026)
claims.note: Merriam-Webster gives \ˈak-sə-ˌlä-tᵊl\ and \ˈak-sə-ˌlät-əl\. The article's respelling matches, though primary stress is on the first syllable (AK-suh-lot-ul), which the article's rendering does not convey.

claims.claim: Native to Mexico
claims.sourceCitation: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group. 2020. Ambystoma mexicanum. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2020: e.T1095A53947343. Assessed 23 October 2019
claims.note: True but vaguer than the source. IUCN lists the native range as Mexico (Ciudad de México) at just 3 locations; Ramos et al. 2025 describe the species as "endemic to Lake Xochimilco, the last remnant of a once-extensive wetland system in the Central Valley of Mexico." "Native to Mexico" undersells how tiny the actual range is.

claims.claim: This "walking fish" is actually a type of salamander
claims.sourceCitation: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group. 2020. Ambystoma mexicanum. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2020: e.T1095A53947343
claims.note: IUCN taxonomy: Class Amphibia, Order Caudata, Family Ambystomatidae, Genus Ambystoma. Joven et al. 2019 treat it as the prime salamander model for regeneration research.

claims.claim: A salamander that never grows up - it stays in its cute larval form for its entire life
claims.sourceCitation: Page RB, Voss SR, Samuels AK, Smith JJ, Putta S, Beachy CK. 2008. Effect of thyroid hormone concentration on the transcriptional response underlying induced metamorphosis in the Mexican axolotl (Ambystoma). BMC Genomics 9:78. doi:10.1186/1471-2164-9-78
claims.note: Two problems. (1) "Never" is too absolute: Page et al. 2008 state "A. mexicanum can be induced to undergo anatomical metamorphosis by administering TH and endocrine factors that function upstream of TH synthesis" - the animal's tissues stay fully responsive to thyroid hormone, it is the HPT axis that is underactive. Merriam-Webster likewise says axolotls "ordinarily live and breed in the larval form without metamorphosing." (2) "Never grows up" conflates morphology with maturity: Joven et al. 2019 describe it as "a fully aquatic paedomorphic animal, meaning that it retains larval features, such as external gills, throughout its entire life span" - it reaches full adult size and breeds normally. The correct word is paedomorphosis, not "stays a baby."

claims.claim: They can regenerate entire limbs
claims.sourceCitation: Joven A, Elewa A, Simon A. 2019. Model systems for regeneration: salamanders. Development 146(14):dev167700. doi:10.1242/dev.167700
claims.note: Joven et al. describe blastema growth by week two, an elbow bend by week three, and note that "1 month after amputation, a salamander limb can regenerate its complex features." Tanaka 2016 (Cell 165:1598-1608) covers the underlying growth control, cell fate programming and positional information, though its abstract discusses appendage regeneration across models rather than naming the axolotl.

claims.claim: They can regenerate spinal cords
claims.sourceCitation: Joven A, Elewa A, Simon A. 2019. Model systems for regeneration: salamanders. Development 146(14):dev167700. doi:10.1242/dev.167700
claims.note: Joven et al.: "spinal cord trauma in salamanders leads to only a transient loss of locomotion," with the central canal restored and new neurons and axons growing through permissive channels formed by ependymoglial cell extensions.

claims.claim: They can regenerate even parts of their brain
claims.sourceCitation: Amamoto R, Lopez Huerta VG, Takahashi E, Dai G, Grant AK, Fu Z, Arlotta P. 2016. Adult axolotls can regenerate original neuronal diversity in response to brain injury. eLife 5:e13998. doi:10.7554/eLife.13998
claims.note: Supported as written, and the article's hedge ("parts of") is the right one. Worth knowing before anyone escalates it: Amamoto et al. found regenerated neurons "acquire functional electrophysiological traits" but that "the original tissue architecture cannot be regenerated" and "regenerated neurons cannot rebuild long-distance circuit" - roughly 70% fewer neurons projected to the olfactory bulb than in controls. The authors say their findings "challenge prior assumptions of functional brain regeneration in salamanders." So the brain regrows tissue and cell diversity, not the original wiring.

claims.claim: They come in beautiful colors like white, black, golden
claims.sourceCitation: Cecil RF, Strohl L, Thomas MK, Schwartz JL, Timoshevskaya N, Smith JJ, Voss SR. 2024. Tyrp1 is the mendelian determinant of the Axolotl (Ambystoma mexicanum) copper mutant. Scientific Reports 14:22399. doi:10.1038/s41598-024-73283-1
claims.note: Cecil et al. name "four different color mutants that are determined by single genes: white, melanoid, albino, and axanthic," plus copper. White = the article's "white," melanoid = "black," golden albino = a form of the albino mutant. Woodcock et al. 2017 pin white to an endothelin 3 (edn3) splicing defect and albino to a 142 bp tyrosinase (tyr) deletion.

claims.claim: They come in even glowing GFP varieties
claims.sourceCitation: Sobkow L, Epperlein H-H, Herklotz S, Straube WL, Tanaka EM. 2006. A germline GFP transgenic axolotl and its use to track cell fate: dual origin of the fin mesenchyme during development and the fate of blood cells during regeneration. Developmental Biology 290(2):386-397. doi:10.1016/j.ydbio.2005.11.037
claims.note: GFP axolotls are real: Sobkow et al. generated "a germline transgenic animal expressing GFP ubiquitously in all tissues examined," the first germline transgene transmission in the axolotl, and the line later reached the hobby. Precision point: GFP fluoresces, it is not bioluminescent. These animals only "glow" under blue or UV excitation, not in ordinary room light.

claims.claim: In the wild, axolotls are critically endangered
claims.sourceCitation: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group. 2020. Ambystoma mexicanum. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2020: e.T1095A53947343. Assessed 23 October 2019, published 2020
claims.note: IUCN lists Critically Endangered under criteria A2abce, assessed 23 October 2019. Population 50 to 1,000 mature individuals, decreasing, severely fragmented, across 3 locations. If you want a harder number in the piece, that 50-1,000 figure is the citable one.

claims.claim: They're very popular in the pet trade
claims.sourceCitation: IUCN SSC Amphibian Specialist Group. 2020. Ambystoma mexicanum. The IUCN Red List of Threatened Species 2020: e.T1095A53947343
claims.note: IUCN's Use and Trade section flags "Pets/display animals" at both national and international scale, alongside research use. Cecil et al. 2024 note that "pet breeders have identified color variants that have not received biological study" and that "commercial and private axolotl collections may harbor genetic variants" useful to research. Context the article omits: Woodcock et al. 2017 showed the laboratory (and by extension hobby) axolotl is "a distinct, hybrid axolotl strain" carrying introgressed tiger salamander DNA, with 88% of wild-type lab animals carrying the tyr_a allele. Captive abundance is therefore not a reservoir for the wild Xochimilco population.

claims.claim: Make sure you have a proper 20+ gallon tank
claims.sourceCitation: Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center, University of Kentucky. Guide to Axolotl Husbandry (accessed 2026)
claims.note: No primary or institutional source states 20 gallons. The nearest authoritative figure runs the other way: the NIH-funded Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center gives "a half gallon (2 liters) of water per axolotl" as an adult minimum and says "two adults in a ten-gallon aquarium" works well, but pairs that with water changes "at least every other day." 20 gallons is a reasonable hobbyist convention for a filtered home tank, not a sourced requirement, and should be presented as such.

claims.claim: Cold water (around 60 to 64°F)
claims.sourceCitation: Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center, University of Kentucky. Guide to Axolotl Husbandry (accessed 2026)
claims.note: AGSC: "We keep our axolotls at 15-18°C (60-65°F). They should never be kept above about 22°C (72°F)." The article's 60-64°F sits inside that band. The more useful number for readers, which the article omits, is the hard ceiling of about 72°F.

claims.claim: Small changes in water temperature, pH, or ammonia levels can cause serious stress or illness
claims.sourceCitation: Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center, University of Kentucky. Guide to Axolotl Husbandry (accessed 2026)
claims.note: The direction is right but "small changes" is not what the source describes. AGSC accepts a pH anywhere "between about 6.5 and 8" and runs its colony across 15-18°C, so small fluctuations inside those bands are not the hazard. The named risks are ammonia and nitrite accumulation (hence "a biological filter that can convert ammonia and nitrites" plus daily to every-other-day water changes) and sustained warmth above about 22°C. AGSC also adds a hazard the article misses entirely: "Never house them in extremely soft or distilled water. They need hard water to help them maintain the integrity of their skin." Note the pH interaction: "if pH is at the high end of this range, monitor ammonia carefully because its toxicity will be greater than at neutral pH."
