corrections.claim: this "walking fish" is actually a type of salamander that never grows up - it stays in its cute larval form for its entire life!
corrections.problem: "Never" is wrong and "never grows up" is imprecise. Page et al. 2008 (BMC Genomics 9:78) state that A. mexicanum "can be induced to undergo anatomical metamorphosis by administering TH and endocrine factors that function upstream of TH synthesis" - the tissues remain fully sensitive to thyroid hormone, it is the hypothalamic-pituitary-thyroid axis that is underactive. Merriam-Webster's own definition hedges with "ordinarily live and breed in the larval form without metamorphosing." Separately, axolotls do grow up: they reach full adult size and breed. What they keep is larval anatomy (external gills, finned tail, aquatic life), which is paedomorphosis, not perpetual infancy.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "this 'walking fish' is actually a type of salamander that keeps its larval body for life. An axolotl reaches full size and breeds while still wearing its feathery external gills and finned tail, a condition biologists call paedomorphosis. It is not that they cannot transform. Their tissues respond perfectly well to thyroid hormone, and researchers can push an axolotl through a full metamorphosis by dosing it. Left alone, they simply never trigger it themselves."

corrections.claim: Axolotls are remarkably sensitive creatures - small changes in water temperature, pH, or ammonia levels can cause serious stress or illness.
corrections.problem: Overstated and misdirected. The Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center at the University of Kentucky accepts a pH anywhere "between about 6.5 and 8" and runs its colony across 15-18°C, so small fluctuations inside those bands are not the danger. The real hazards it names are ammonia and nitrite accumulation and sustained warmth above about 22°C (72°F). AGSC also flags a risk the article never mentions: "Never house them in extremely soft or distilled water. They need hard water to help them maintain the integrity of their skin."
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "Axolotls are hardy when the basics are right and fragile when they are not. Two things actually hurt them: heat and ammonia. The Ambystoma Genetic Stock Center at the University of Kentucky keeps its colony at 15 to 18°C (60 to 65°F) and warns they should never be kept above about 22°C (72°F). pH anywhere from 6.5 to 8 is fine, but the higher the pH, the more toxic any ammonia in the tank becomes, so a properly cycled biological filter and regular water changes matter far more than chasing an exact number. One more thing keepers miss: axolotls need hard water. Extremely soft or distilled water damages their skin."

corrections.claim: make sure you have a proper 20+ gallon tank
corrections.problem: No primary or institutional source states 20 gallons, and the nearest authoritative figure is much smaller. AGSC gives "a half gallon (2 liters) of water per axolotl" as an adult minimum and notes "two adults in a ten-gallon aquarium" works well, but pairs that with water changes "at least every other day." Stating 20 gallons as a flat requirement presents a hobbyist convention as a sourced fact, which is exactly the pattern this site's standard is meant to catch.
corrections.suggestedFix: Replace with: "make sure you have a tank of at least 20 gallons, the usual hobbyist recommendation, and cold water (around 60 to 64°F, never above about 72°F). The volume is not magic. Research colonies house adults in as little as half a gallon of water each, but they change that water every day or two. In a home tank the extra volume is what keeps ammonia from spiking between water changes."

verdicts.problem: No defect. Fetched an 11-page PDF that is genuinely 'Do honey badgers and greater honeyguide birds cooperate to access bees' nests? Ecological evidence and honey-hunter accounts' by van der Wal, Afan, Anyawire, Begg, Begg et al. Abstract verbatim: 'We find that the scientific evidence relies on incomplete and second-hand accounts and does not convincingly indicate that the two species cooperate,' drawn from '394 interviews with honey-hunters in 11 communities across nine African countries.' Staged-footage claim confirmed verbatim: the 1974 film 'Animals Are Beautiful People' footage 'was in fact entirely staged using a tame badger trained to follow a taxidermic model of a bird on a fishing line.' Brain claim confirmed verbatim: 'Badgers have relatively large brains that may allow them to learn to exploit new food sources (Benson-Amram et al., 2016; Sheppey & Bernard, 1984).' CAVEAT WORTH KNOWING: this NSF copy is the early-view version, whose running head still carries unassigned placeholders instead of volume and pages, so the PDF itself cannot confirm '321:22-32'. I verified the final pagination independently through the Crossref record for the paper's DOI (10.1111/jzo.13093), which returns Journal of Zoology, volume 321, pages 22-32, 2023. Citation is therefore correct. Two trivia corrections to the researcher's note, neither affecting the citation: the author list is 26 names, not 25, and the interviews spanned 11 communities across nine countries.

No defect. Title, authors (Drabeck, Dean, Jansa), journal (Toxicon), year (2015), volume (99) and pages (68-72) all match exactly. Abstract confirms the researcher's three caveats: honey badgers, hedgehogs and pigs 'have independently acquired functionally equivalent amino acid replacements' at the toxin-binding site, while mongooses achieve resistance by a different route involving glycosylation; the receptor in question is the target of snake alpha-neurotoxins, and elapids are named explicitly. This supports the 'overstated' verdict on the mongoose framing and on extending an elapid-specific mechanism to puff adder (viper) bites.

No defect. Header reads 'J. Zool., Lond. (2003) 260, 301-316' with authors C.M. Begg, K.S. Begg, J.T. Du Toit and M.G.L. Mills, matching the citation exactly. Every figure attributed to it verified in the text: '3324 food items were identified'; springhare 22.2%, mole snake 21.4%, puff adder 12.5%, Cape cobra 10.5% of biomass; 'All small mammals, small reptiles and large reptiles were eaten entirely, including the heads of poisonous snakes.' The load-bearing beehive quote is verbatim: two study animals were watched 'breaking into 13 bee hives over 37 visits... On 61% of the visits the swarm's defence was sufficient to chase off the honey badgers,' plus 'honey badgers were twice observed to unsuccessfully attempt to break into bee hives' - so the 'wrong' verdict on the zero-hesitation beehive claim is correctly grounded. Springhare specialisation confirmed, including the cub detail: 'While this female's cub was observed to use this same hunting technique successfully once independent of her mother, this was not observed in other habituated honey badgers.' A full-text search for 'mamba' returns zero hits, independently confirming the 'unverifiable' verdict on mambas.

No defect. Header reads 'J. Zool., Lond. (2005) 265, 17-22' with the same four authors, matching exactly. Abstract confirms 'The honey badger is a non-social species and only the mother rears the young' and 'the unusually small litter size of one cub.' The litter-size rebuttal is verbatim: the study 'provides no evidence for the reported litter sizes of 1-4 cubs (mean = 2.5; Neal & Cheeseman, 1996; Johnson et al., 2000).' Independence figures confirmed: cubs 'remained with their mothers for at least 12-16 months (n=7; range = 12-22 months)', with means of 14.2 months for males and 14.6 for females. Adult mortality confirmed as '34% +/- 6% (SE)', and the hyaena-den remains are in the text. Fully supports both the 'wrong' verdict on litter size and the 'overstated' verdict on 18-24 month dependency.

No defect. This is the single most load-bearing source in the article (nine claims) and it holds up on every one. Masthead reads 'MAMMALIAN SPECIES No. 721, pp. 1-8, 3 figs. Mellivora capensis. By Jana M. Vanderhaar and Yeen Ten Hwang, Published 30 July 2003 by the American Society of Mammalogists' - matches 721:1-8, 2003. (The text renders as cid-encoded glyphs; I decoded it rather than trusting a summary.) Verified verbatim: 'Near the throat, skin is 6 mm thick (Kingdon 1977)'; skin prevents 'firmly grasping it and allowing honey badgers to turn in their skin and bite the attacker'; 'Skin is impervious to stings of bees, fangs of snakes, and teeth of dogs (Blumenbach 1825; Stevenson-Hamilton 1947)'; 'Average length of nails is ca. 32 mm. The middle one is longest, ca. 38 mm, and the smallest outer one is <25 mm'; 'Each anal gland measures ca. 30 by 20 mm', secretion 'is yellow and looks similar to liquid mustard, and its smell can be perceived at a distance of >=45 m', 'Anal pouch is everted whenever honey badgers become excited (Kingdon 1977); fluid is dribbled, not squirted (Estes 1991)'; 'Anal secretions may be used to fumigate insects when robbing nests of bees'; 'honey badgers cannot run quickly'; 'Honey badgers are good swimmers and chase turtles underwater'; 'carapaces of turtles... are peeled away to expose the softer inner parts'; females ca. 10 km/day and males ca. 27 km/day (Kruuk and Mills 1983); mass 9.2 kg (7.7-10.5, n=9) males and 8.9 kg (6.2-13.6, n=5) females. I also ran targeted searches for 'porcupine', 'quills' and 'machete': zero hits for quills and machete, and 'porcupine' appears only as a source of abandoned burrows. That independently confirms the 'overstated' verdict - the machete detail really is absent from this source.

No defect in the citation. Resolves to a 13-page copy of the genuine assessment (carrying DOI 10.2305/IUCN.UK.2016-1.RLTS.T41629A45210107.en), matching e.T41629A45210107, 2016, Do Linh San, Begg, Begg and Abramov. Note it is a ResearchGate-uploaded mirror rather than iucnredlist.org, but the content is the authentic assessment text. Verified verbatim: Family Mustelidae; range 'through most of sub-Saharan Africa... and outside Africa through Arabia, Iran and western Asia to Middle Asia (Turkmenistan, Uzbekistan), the Indian peninsula and Nepal'; 'Large carnivores such as Lion (Panthera leo) and Leopard (Panthera pardus) prey on Honey Badger adults and cubs, while cubs are also killed by Black-backed Jackals'; 'Honey Badgers are essentially nocturnal, but may be active during the day in areas where there is little human disturbance'; they 'may pirate food from other carnivores and will also scavenge from the kills of larger animals'; Least Concern with 'Current Population Trend: Decreasing'; 'evidence to suggest they have gone locally extinct in many areas through poisoning'; 'Small litter size (generally one cub)'; density 0.03 adult/km2 in Kgalagadi. ONE CORRECTION to the researcher's note, not to the source: the note says IUCN lists 'subfamily Mellivorinae', but the taxonomy block lists only Family Mustelidae and the string 'Mellivorinae' does not appear anywhere in the document. The claim actually cited (weasel family plus range) is fully supported, so the source stands; only the annotation overreaches.

No defect. Title, authors (Spottiswoode, Begg, Begg), journal (Science), year (2016), volume (353) and pages (387-389) all match exactly. Abstract confirms the specific figures cited: the specialised honey-hunters' call raised the probability of being guided from about 33% to 66%, and of finding a bees' nest from 17% to 54%.

No defect. Live SANBI page on Mellivora capensis. Confirms both claims cited to it: the honey badger was named the 'most fearless animal in the world' in the 2002 edition of the Guinness Book of World Records, and it stands 'at a height of approximately 25-30cm at the shoulders' (10-12 inches). The page's own wording is past-tense and edition-specific, which supports the researcher's caveat that the article's present-tense 'officially named' overstates a retired print accolade.

No defect. Live Honey Badger Research Project site by Colleen and Keith Begg. Supports the claim it was cited for, and supports the 'overstated' verdict, with the verbatim line: 'A honey badger bitten on the face by the highly cytotoxic puff adder showed signs of severe pain but recovered fully within five hours (Begg & Begg pers. obs.)' - hours of envenomation, not the brief collapse-and-shake-it-off the article describes. Same domain also hosts the two Begg PDFs cited above, both of which resolved.

No defect. Live University of Cambridge research story dated 29 June 2023, quoting van der Wal, Cram, Spottiswoode and Wood. The attributed quote is verbatim: 'While researching honeyguides, we've been guided to bees' nests by honeyguide birds thousands of times, but none of us have ever seen a bird and a badger interact to find honey.' Correctly paired with the 2023 Journal of Zoology paper it publicises.

No defect. Live article on honey badger intelligence. Confirms Stoffel, Brian Jones and the Moholoholo Rehabilitation Centre, and both quotes used to mark the cognition claim as overstated: 'There are simply no studies of honey badger cognition anywhere in the scientific literature,' and Cambridge evolutionary primatologist William McGrew on the footage: 'Either honey badgers have been under-estimated, or this is a one-off genius honey badger, or it is a hoax.' Popular-science outlet rather than peer-reviewed, but it is cited only for the anecdote and for the absence of studies, which is exactly what it establishes.

curationRule.rationale: Site median is 2 sources per article; 175 of 350 have exactly 2 and only 10 exceed 6. The agents proposed 8 to 30 because the prompt asked for a source behind every load-bearing claim, which produces a research bibliography rather than a reading-list. The full set stays here as working notes; only the curated few belong in the article.
curationRule.ranking: Sources behind a correction first, since those are the ones the article got wrong and a reader may want to check. Then sources backing the most claims. Cap at 5.

resolutionPass.approach: Overstated claims rewritten to what the source actually supports, keeping the correction visible in the prose rather than quietly deleting the claim. Unverifiable claims either softened to the sourced generality or stated as unsourced, with the reason given. Source blocks left at the 5-cap; new citations added only where an edit introduced a genuinely new sourcing need.
